units.name: Vector similarity: cosine, dot product, L2
units.question: How close is a chunk's embedding to the query's embedding?
units.formula_latex: \cos(q,d)=\frac{q\cdot d}{\lVert q\rVert\,\lVert d\rVert}\qquad q\cdot d=\sum_{i=1}^{n}q_i d_i\qquad \lVert q-d\rVert_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(q_i-d_i)^2}\qquad \text{unit vectors: } \lVert q-d\rVert_2^2=2-2\cos(q,d)

symbols.q: The query turned into a list of n numbers (its embedding). One arrow from the origin to a point in n-dimensional space.
symbols.d: One chunk turned into a list of n numbers by the same embedding model. Every chunk in the index is one such arrow.
symbols.n: The embedding dimension: how many numbers each vector has (for example 768 or 1536). The teaching picture uses n = 2 so the arrows can be drawn.
symbols.q_i, d_i: The i-th number of the query and of the chunk. Position i means the same thing in both vectors, because one model made both.
symbols.q . d (dot product): Multiply the two vectors position by position and add all the products. It is large when both vectors point the same way AND are long.
symbols.||q||, ||d|| (length, L2 norm): The length of the arrow: the square root of the sum of its squared numbers. It says how long the arrow is, not where it points.
symbols.cos(q,d): The dot product divided by both lengths. It cancels length, so only the angle between the arrows is left: 1 = same direction, 0 = at right angles, -1 = opposite.
symbols.||q - d||_2 (L2 / Euclidean distance): The straight-line distance between the two arrow tips. It is 0 when the vectors are equal, and it grows with both angle and length difference. Smaller = closer, so a retriever ranks by ascending distance.
symbols.2 - 2cos(q,d): For two vectors of length 1 the squared L2 distance equals 2 minus twice the cosine. So on unit vectors L2 and cosine give the same ranking (smaller distance = larger cosine), and dot = cosine.

units.inputs: q: query vector; docs: list of chunk vectors; normalise: whether every vector is first scaled to length 1 (all numbers given by the user or by an embedding model; the demo uses 2-D toy vectors).
units.range: cosine in [-1, 1]; dot product unbounded (equals cosine when both lengths are 1); L2 distance in [0, infinity), and in [0, 2] when both vectors have length 1.
units.higher_is_better: cosine and dot: yes; L2: no (smaller distance = closer). Rank L2 ascending.

worked_example.setup: Toy 2-D vectors (invented for teaching, not from a real model). Query q = (0.8, 0.6), length 1. Chunk A = (0.6, 0.8): close to q, length 1. Chunk B = (2.4, 1.8) = 3q: exactly the same direction, three times as long. Chunk C = (2.4, 0): a different direction (about 37 degrees away), length 2.4.
steps: Rank by cosine: B (1.0), A (0.96), C (0.8). Rank by dot: B (3.0), C (1.92), A (0.96). Rank by L2 (smallest first): A (0.283), C (1.709), B (2.0). Three different orders from the same vectors.

Normalise every vector to length 1: B becomes q (cos 1, dot 1, L2 0), C becomes (1, 0) (cos 0.8, dot 0.8, L2 0.632), A is unchanged. All three measures now give B, A, C. Check: L2^2 for C = 0.4 = 2 - 2*0.8.

blind_spots: Dot product rewards length: a long vector (chunk C, length 2.4) can beat a better-aimed short one (chunk A). Whether embedding length carries meaning depends on the model; for most text-embedding models it does not.
L2 punishes length difference: chunk B has exactly the query's direction but is ranked last, because it is far away in space.
Cosine ignores length completely, so it cannot tell a short vector from a long one; if length does carry signal (for example confidence or term frequency) cosine throws it away.

In high dimension, distances between random-looking vectors concentrate (everything looks about equally far); scores from one metric are not comparable with scores from another or across embedding models.
The metric must match the one the embedding model was trained with (unverified for any specific model; check the model card). The index metric (HNSW, FAISS) must also be set to it.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use cosine when only direction should matter, the safe default for text embeddings. If the embedding model returns unit-length vectors (many do; check the model card, unverified here), dot product, cosine and L2 give identical rankings and dot is the cheapest, so vector indexes often use it. Use raw dot product (maximum inner product search) only when length is meaningful to the model. Use L2 when the model was trained with it or when absolute position matters (clusters, k-means, anomaly distance). Neighbours: BM25 scores words not vectors; ColBERT MaxSim applies one of these measures per token; ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) speed up the search but need the metric chosen first.

source.cite: Manning, Raghavan & Schutze (2008) Introduction to Information Retrieval, section 6.3.1 'Dot products' (cosine = dot product of length-normalised vectors); L2 identity derived and checked in code.

units.notes: Evidenced: cosine definition and 'cosine = dot product of the length-normalised vectors' read in IR-book 6.3.1 (equations 24-25 there); Pinecone's comparison table (cosine: direction only; dot and L2: magnitude and direction) read. Derived: L2^2 = 2-2cos on unit vectors (algebra, numerically checked for all three chunks). Not checked: which specific embedding models return unit vectors (claims about models are marked unverified). Toy vectors are ours, 2-D only; real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions and the 2-D picture hides concentration of distances.

units.name: Embeddings and the embedding space
units.question: How does text become a point in space?
units.formula_latex: \vec e(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\vec h_i,\quad \vec h_i=f_\theta(t_1,\dots,t_n)_i\qquad\text{then compare texts by }\ \cos(\vec e(x),\vec e(y))=\frac{\vec e(x)\cdot\vec e(y)}{\lVert\vec e(x)\rVert\,\lVert\vec e(y)\rVert}

symbols.x, y: Two pieces of text: a query and a chunk, or two chunks.
symbols.t_1 ... t_n: The tokens (word pieces) of the text. The text is cut into n tokens before it enters the model.
symbols.f_theta: The embedding model, for example a BERT-style Transformer with learned weights theta. It reads all tokens together and gives each token a vector that depends on its context.
symbols.h_i: The output vector of token i, a list of d numbers (d is often 384, 768 or 1024). Its direction encodes meaning.
symbols.e(x): The embedding of the whole text: one vector of d numbers, the point that stands for x in the space. Mean pooling (average of the h_i) is the default in Sentence-BERT; other models use the first token or a special pooling.
symbols.1/n and the sum: Mean pooling: add up the n token vectors and divide by n. Every token counts the same.
symbols.cos(e(x), e(y)): Cosine similarity: the angle between two points seen from the origin. 1 = same direction (same meaning), 0 = unrelated, -1 = opposite. See the Vector Similarity unit.
symbols.embedding space: The d-dimensional space in which all texts live. Training (for example with sentence pairs and siamese networks) pulls texts with similar meaning close together and pushes others apart.

units.inputs: A text (query or chunk), an embedding model with fixed weights, and a similarity function. The same model must embed the query and the chunks.
units.range: The embedding is d real numbers; cosine similarity of two embeddings is between -1 and 1 (for most text models in practice mostly positive; unverified for a given model). Values are only comparable within one model.

worked_example.setup: Toy, invented: 3-dimensional token vectors written by hand (NOT output of a real model; real models use hundreds of dimensions and context-dependent vectors). Three texts: A = 'the cat sat on the mat', B = 'the kitten slept on the rug', C = 'stock prices fell'. The vector of 'the' is 0 (a stop word), 'cat' = (0.9, 0.1, 0.0), 'kitten' = (0.85, 0.2, 0.05), 'sat' = (0.1, 0.8, 0.1), 'slept' = (0.15, 0.75, 0.2), 'on' = (0, 0.1, 0.1), 'mat' = (0.5, 0.3, 0), 'rug' = (0.55, 0.25, 0.05), 'stock' = (0, 0, 0.95), 'prices' = (0, 0.05, 0.9), 'fell' = (0, 0.1, 0.8).
steps: Mean pooling of A (6 tokens): e(A) = sum / 6 = [0.25, 0.2167, 0.0333].
Mean pooling of B (6 tokens): e(B) = [0.2583, 0.2167, 0.0667]. Mean pooling of C (3 tokens): e(C) = [0.0, 0.05, 0.8833].
Cosine A-B = 0.9954. Cosine A-C = 0.1369. Cosine B-C = 0.2293.

A and B share only the words 'the' and 'on' (word overlap, Jaccard = 0.25), yet their embeddings point almost the same way. This is the point of an embedding: similar meaning gives close points even without shared words (in our toy because we put cat/kitten and mat/rug close by hand; a real model learns this from data).

blind_spots: The model decides what 'similar' means: it is trained for one notion (for example sentence meaning); it may rate 'the drug is safe' and 'the drug is not safe' as very close, because they share almost all words and topic. Negation, numbers and exact names are typical weak spots (the Sentence-BERT paper reports results on similarity benchmarks only; the negation claim is general experience, unverified here).

Mean pooling treats all tokens alike and loses word order information beyond what the Transformer already encoded; long texts are squeezed into one vector and the model has a maximum input length (texts beyond it are cut).
Different models have different spaces: vectors from two models cannot be compared, and changing the model means re-embedding the whole index.
Domain shift: a model trained on general text may separate legal or medical terms badly. Test on your own queries.
Not interpretable: the individual dimensions have no name; you only see distances. Rare words and spellings can be mapped to unexpected places.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Embeddings are the input of dense retrieval: embed chunks once, embed the query at question time, rank by cosine or dot product (see Vector Similarity), speed up with HNSW. Use BM25 / TF-IDF when exact words matter. Use a cross-encoder reranker when you can afford to read query and passage together. Use HyDE when the query is too short or too unlike the documents to embed well.

source.cite: Reimers, N. & Gurevych, I. (2019) Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks. EMNLP 2019, arXiv:1908.10084. Formula check 2026-10-08 in the arXiv PDF: Sec. 3 'Model', PDF p.3: 'SBERT adds a pooling operation to the output of BERT / RoBERTa ... three pooling strategies: CLS-token, the mean of all output vectors (MEAN-strategy), max-over-time (MAX-strategy). The default configuration is MEAN', and the embeddings 'can be compared with cosine-similarity'; Sec. 4, PDF p.4: 'we always use cosine-similarity to compare the similarity between two sentence embeddings'. The paper names cosine similarity but does not print its equation; the cosine formula shown is its standard definition. The toy vectors are ours.

units.name: TF-IDF
units.question: Which words are distinctive for a document?

symbols.tf(t,d): Term frequency: how many times word t appears in document d. The more often, the more the document is about t. (Variants use a log or divide by document length; we use the raw count.)
symbols.N: The number of documents in the collection.
symbols.n(t): Document frequency: in how many documents word t appears at least once.
symbols.idf(t): Inverse document frequency: ln(N / n(t)). A word in every document gets ln(1) = 0, a worthless word. A word in one document out of many gets a large value. It measures how distinctive the word is for the collection. (Spärck Jones 1972 introduced the idea; the log form is the common choice.)
symbols.tfidf(t,d): The product: high when the word is frequent in this document AND rare in the collection. It is the weight of word t in the vector of document d.
symbols.score(q,d): A simple query score: add up the tf-idf of the query words in the document. Often the query and document vectors are instead compared with cosine similarity.
symbols.q: The query as a bag of words.

units.inputs: The collection of N tokenised documents (counts of each word per document and document frequencies), and a query as a list of words.
units.range: tf-idf >= 0 and unbounded above. idf is between 0 (word in every document) and ln(N) (word in one document). Scores only compare within one query and one collection.

worked_example.setup: Toy collection (invented), N = 4 documents: d1 = 'graph retrieval uses a graph of entities'; d2 = 'vector retrieval uses embeddings'; d3 = 'the graph of the corpus has communities'; d4 = 'retrieval of the answer uses the context'. Raw term counts, natural log. Query: 'graph retrieval'.
steps: Document frequencies n(t): graph = 2, retrieval = 3, the = 2, entities = 1, uses = 3.
idf = ln(4 / n): graph = 0.6931, retrieval = 0.2877, the = 0.6931, entities = 1.3863, uses = 0.2877. 'entities' (1 document) is the most distinctive; 'retrieval' and 'uses' (3 documents) the least.
In d1: tf(graph) = 2, tf(retrieval) = 1. tfidf(graph, d1) = 2 * 0.6931 = 1.3863; tfidf(retrieval, d1) = 1 * 0.2877 = 0.2877; tfidf(entities, d1) = 1.3863.
Query 'graph retrieval', score = sum of tf-idf: d1 = 1.674, d2 = 0.2877, d3 = 0.6931, d4 = 0.2877. Ranking: d1 > d3 > d2 > d4.

Compare with the raw count of query words: d1 = 3, d2 = 1, d3 = 1, d4 = 1. In the raw count d4 ties with d3 and d2 (each 1), but tf-idf separates them because 'graph' (in 2 documents) is worth more than 'retrieval' (in 3 documents): d3 = 0.6931 (only 'graph'), d2 and d4 = 0.2877 (only 'retrieval').

blind_spots: No meaning: 'car' never matches 'automobile'; only the exact words (after stemming) count.

tf grows without a ceiling: a document that repeats a word 50 times scores 50 times higher, so keyword stuffing and long documents are favoured. BM25 adds saturation and length normalisation to fix exactly this.
No length normalisation in the raw form: long documents contain more words and get larger sums. Common fix: cosine-normalise the vectors, or use BM25.

idf depends on the collection: in a tiny or topic-narrow collection, a word that matters to every document gets idf near 0 and vanishes (for example 'graph' in a corpus about graphs). Adding or removing documents changes all weights.
Word order and phrases are ignored (bag of words), and an idf of 0 for a word in all documents also removes it when it is the whole query.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use TF-IDF for a cheap sparse baseline, for keyword extraction (which words are distinctive of a document), and to understand BM25, its improved descendant: BM25 saturates tf and normalises length, so prefer BM25 for ranking chunks. Use embeddings (dense) when the query and the answer use different words for the same idea. Hybrid retrieval combines a sparse score (BM25 or TF-IDF) with a dense score (see RRF fusion).

source.cite: Manning, C. D., Raghavan, P. & Schuetze, H. (6.8) tf-idf_{t,d} = tf_{t,d} x idf_t; Eq. (6.9) Score(q,d) = sum over t in q of tf-idf_{t,d}; the text says 'the precise base of the logarithm is not material to ranking'. A textbook, so primary-ish, not the original paper. Spaerck Jones, K. (1972) A statistical interpretation of term specificity and its application in retrieval. Journal of Documentation 28(1), 11-21 (read in the 2004 reprint, J. Doc. 60(5) 493-502, PDF p.6): her weight is f(N) - f(n) + 1 with f(n) = m such that 2^(m-1) < n <= 2^m, i.e. a rounded base-2 log ratio plus 1, the origin of idf but not the ln(N/n) form shown. Salton & Buckley (1988) was not opened.

units.name: BM25 (k1 saturation and b length normalisation)
units.question: How do we score keyword match with saturation and length normalisation?

symbols.Q, t: The query is a bag of words. t is one query word. The score adds up one contribution per query word.
symbols.D: One chunk (document) of text in the index.
symbols.f(t,D): Term frequency: how many times word t appears in chunk D. A count, 0, 1, 2, ...
symbols.|D|: Length of chunk D in words (tokens).
symbols.avgdl: Average chunk length over the whole collection. It is the yardstick: a chunk of exactly this length is 'normal'.
symbols.N: How many chunks the collection has.
symbols.n(t): In how many chunks the word t appears at least once (document frequency). A common word has a large n(t), a rare word a small one.
symbols.IDF(t): Inverse document frequency: how much one match on t is worth. Rare word = high weight, common word = low weight. (This is the one TF-IDF idea we need here; TF-IDF itself gets its own unit.) The +1 inside the ln (Lucene form) keeps it above 0.
symbols.k1: Saturation knob, usually 1.2 to 2.0. It sets how fast extra repeats stop helping. k1 = 0: only 'is the word there' counts. Large k1: the score keeps growing almost linearly with the count. Upper limit of one word's tf part is (k1 + 1).
symbols.b: Length-normalisation knob between 0 and 1, usually 0.75. b = 0: chunk length is ignored. b = 1: full normalisation, a chunk twice as long as average must show twice the count to look the same.
symbols.1 - b + b*|D|/avgdl: The length factor. It is 1 for an average-length chunk, above 1 for a longer chunk (counts are discounted), below 1 for a shorter one (counts are boosted). b decides how strongly length matters.
symbols.f(k1+1) / (f + k1*lengthfactor): The saturating tf part. It starts at 0 for f = 0, rises fast for the first repeats, then flattens towards the ceiling k1 + 1. Half of the ceiling is reached when f equals k1 times the length factor.

units.inputs: Query words; for each chunk: count of each query word f(t,D) and length |D|; collection statistics N, avgdl and n(t) per word; the two knobs k1 and b.
units.range: Score >= 0 and unbounded above (it grows with the number of query words and their IDF). Per word the tf part is below k1 + 1. Scores are only comparable within one query on one collection.

worked_example.setup: Toy collection of N = 1000 chunks with avgdl = 100 words (invented for teaching). Query: 'graph retrieval'. 'graph' is in 100 chunks, 'retrieval' in 10. k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75. Chunk A: length 100, graph x3, retrieval x1. Chunk B: length 400, graph x6, retrieval x2. Chunk C: length 50, graph x1, retrieval x1.
steps: IDF (rare words weigh more): N = 1000 chunks. 'graph' is in 100 chunks: IDF = ln(1 + (1000-100+0.5)/(100+0.5)) = 2.299. 'retrieval' is in 10 chunks: IDF = ln(1 + (1000-10+0.5)/(10+0.5)) = 4.557.
Ranking with k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75: C (8.619) > A (8.169) > B (6.464). B repeats 'graph' 6 times but is 4 times longer than average, so it is demoted.
Saturation: chunk B says 'graph' twice as often as A (6 vs 3) but its graph part is only 1.333 vs 1.571 (not 2x). With b = 0 (no length normalisation) B jumps to first: B 10.480 > A 8.169 > C 6.856.

blind_spots: No meaning: 'car' never matches 'automobile'. Only the exact (stemmed) word counts; this is why dense retrieval and hybrid search exist.
Words are independent (bag of words): word order and phrases are ignored.

One k1 and b for all fields and all queries; the defaults (1.2, 0.75) are not tuned to your corpus. For chunks of a similar fixed length (typical RAG chunking), length normalisation matters little (unverified in practice).

Scores are not on a fixed scale: the score depends on N, avgdl and the query. You cannot compare BM25 scores across queries, or add them to cosine scores without normalising (see the hybrid search notes and RRF).
IDF depends on the collection: a small or skewed index gives noisy IDF values, and very common words get a weight near 0.
The saturation cap helps against keyword stuffing, but it does not remove it: a chunk that repeats a rare word 40 times still reaches almost the ceiling (k1 + 1) times IDF.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use BM25 when exact words matter: names, codes, rare technical terms, quoted phrases, and as the full-text half of hybrid search (BM25 + vector, fused by normalised scores or RRF; see Notes/02 Vector Similarity Search and Hybrid Search - Essential GraphRAG). Use dense vector similarity when the query and the answer use different words for the same idea. Plain TF-IDF (own unit later) is BM25's ancestor: its tf part grows without a ceiling and has no length knob. BM25 needs no training and no GPU, which makes it a strong, cheap baseline.

source.cite: Robertson & Zaragoza (2009) The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond, Foundations and Trends in IR 3(4). Read by personal-2f (2026-10-08): classic IDF = log((N-n+0.5)/(n+0.5)) with no +1 (Eq. 3.3, p.349); Eq. 3.15 has no (k1+1) in the numerator (it does not change the ranking, Sec. 3.5.1); suggested ranges 0.5<b<0.8 and 1.2<k1<2 (p.360); b=0.75 is a library default, not stated there. We show the Lucene/Elasticsearch variant (IDF with +1, (k1+1) in the numerator, b=0.75); saturation reading from Elastic 'Practical BM25, part 2'.

units.notes: Inferred, not evidenced: formula and parameter defaults read in secondary sources (Wikipedia 'Okapi BM25', Elastic Practical BM25 part 2); the Robertson-Zaragoza page numbers above were read by another session; our IDF and (k1+1) numerator are the Lucene variant, not the paper's. All numbers computed in code (demos/bm25.js is the same maths; scenes/algorithms/bm25.py recomputes). The corpus, counts and lengths are invented for teaching. Variants exist (Lucene IDF with +1, classic Robertson-Sparck Jones IDF without it, BM25+, BM25L); we show the Lucene/Elasticsearch form. TF-IDF is mentioned in one line only; its own unit follows in batch 2.

units.name: Hybrid fusion: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
units.question: How do we merge two ranked lists whose scores are not comparable?

symbols.d: One document (or chunk). The same chunk may appear in the keyword list and in the vector list.
symbols.R: The set of ranked lists to merge. In hybrid RAG search there are two: the keyword (BM25) list and the vector (cosine) list. More lists are allowed.
symbols.r: One ranked list from R, for example the BM25 list. We only use its order, never its scores.
symbols.r(d): The rank of document d in list r: 1 for the first place, 2 for the second, and so on. A smaller number is a better place.
symbols.k: A constant added to every rank before taking the reciprocal. It decides how fast the reward falls from rank 1 to rank 2 and further down. The paper fixes k = 60 in a pilot study and never changes it. With k = 0 the first place is worth twice the second; with k = 60 it is worth only about 1.02 times the second.
symbols.1/(k + r(d)): The reward a document earns from one list. Always positive, always smaller for a worse rank, never zero for a low rank (the paper's intuition: the importance of lower-ranked documents does not vanish, as it would with an exponential).
symbols.sum over r in R: Add the rewards from all lists. A document that is good in both lists collects two big rewards; a document that is first in only one list collects one big and one small reward.
symbols.RRF(d): The fused score. Sort all documents by it, largest first. The value is only meaningful inside one query: it is not a probability and not comparable between queries.

units.inputs: The ranked lists (here two: BM25 and cosine, given as raw scores from which only the order is used) and the constant k (default 60). Documents missing from a list: the paper treats each ranking as a permutation of all documents; a common implementation skips the missing term (unverified for any specific engine).
units.range: Each term lies in (0, 1/(k+1)]. With two lists the fused score lies below 2/(k+1) (0.0328 for k = 60). The number itself has no meaning; only the order matters.
units.higher_is_better: yes (rank documents by descending RRF score)

worked_example.setup: Five chunks A-E (toy numbers, invented for teaching, not from a real index). BM25 scores: A 14.2, B 9.6, C 7.1, D 3.4, E 1.2. Cosine scores: A 0.79, B 0.82, C 0.80, D 0.74, E 0.84. So the BM25 ranks are A1 B2 C3 D4 E5 and the cosine ranks are E1 B2 C3 A4 D5. k = 60.
steps: Why not add the scores? BM25 is unbounded (here 1.2 to 14.2) while cosine lives in a narrow band (0.74 to 0.84). The sum A = 14.2 + 0.79 = 14.99 ... E = 1.2 + 0.84 = 2.04 gives the order A, B, C, D, E: exactly the BM25 order. The cosine list has no effect. Divide the BM25 scores by 100 and the sum follows the cosine list instead. The result depends on the units.
Sort: B (0.032258), A (0.032018), E (0.031778), C (0.031746), D (0.031010). B wins because it is second in both lists; A is first in one list but fourth in the other.

Effect of k: with k = 0 the scores are A 1.25, E 1.2, B 1.0, C 0.667, D 0.45, so the order is A, E, B, C, D (the single first places win). With k = 60 the order is B, A, E, C, D (agreement wins). With k = 1000 the scores differ only in the 6th decimal place.

blind_spots: Scores are thrown away. A document that is far ahead in one list (BM25 14.2 against 9.6) earns the same reward as one that is barely ahead; strong confidence is not rewarded.
Near-ties are fragile. In the example B beats A by 0.00024; a different k or one more list can flip it. Treat small gaps as ties.

A large k flattens everything: with k = 1000 all five scores agree to three significant digits and the order is decided by tiny differences. A small k (0, 1) turns the method into 'whoever is first in any list wins'.
The constant k = 60 was fixed in a pilot on 30 TREC systems, and the paper says the choice 'was not critical'. It is not tuned for RAG chunk lists or embedding retrievers (unverified for them).
Equal weights: every list counts the same. If the vector list is much better than the keyword list for your data, plain RRF cannot say so (weighted variants exist; not checked here).
A document that is in only one list can still rank high; the paper's formula assumes each list ranks all documents, so how absent documents are handled is an implementation choice (unverified).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use RRF when you merge lists from retrievers whose scores live on different scales (BM25 + dense vectors, or several query rewrites as in RAG-Fusion) and you have no labelled data to tune weights. Use weighted score fusion (min-max or max normalisation, then a weighted sum) when you have labels to tune the weight and the scores carry real confidence; the course note 'Essential GraphRAG 02' uses dividing by the highest score. Use a cross-encoder reranker after fusion when the top of the list must be very accurate: RRF only merges, it does not read the text. Neighbours: BM25 and vector similarity make the lists; Condorcet Fuse and CombMNZ are the older fusion methods the paper beats; MMR re-orders for diversity, not for fusion.

source.cite: Cormack, G. V., Clarke, C. L. A., Buettcher, S. (2009) Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods. SIGIR '09, pp. 758-759.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in the paper PDF, 2 pages, converted with markitdown): the formula RRFscore(d) = sum over r in R of 1/(k + r(d)); 'k = 60 was fixed during a pilot investigation and not altered'; Table 1 (MAP of RRF over 30 systems, TREC topics 351-400): k = 0 .2072, 10 .2123, 20 .2134, 30 .2139, 40 .2138, 50 .2144, 60 .2145, 70 .2146, 80 .2147, 90 .2145, 100 .2142, 500 .2098, so k = 60 is near-optimal but not the maximum (80) and 'the choice was not critical'; the paper's intuition that k 'mitigates the impact of high rankings by outlier systems'. Computed in code (Python and node): every score, rank and order in the worked example. Ours: the toy scores and chunk names; the claim that the raw sum follows BM25 is computed for these numbers only. Course note: Essential GraphRAG 02 names the scale problem and fixes it by dividing by the top score; it does not cover RRF. Not checked: how specific engines treat documents absent from a list.

units.name: Hybrid fusion: weighted (convex) combination and score normalisation
units.question: How do we blend dense and sparse scores on one scale?

symbols.f_Convex(q,d): The final hybrid score of document d for query q. Documents are sorted by it, highest first.
symbols.f_Sem(q,d): The dense (semantic) score, for example cosine similarity between query and document embeddings. It usually lies between -1 and 1.
symbols.f_Lex(q,d): The sparse (lexical) score, for example BM25. It has no fixed upper limit; it grows with the number of matching query terms and with term rarity.
symbols.alpha: The mixing weight between 0 and 1, the only parameter. alpha = 1 means use dense scores only; alpha = 0 means lexical only; alpha = 0.5 means equal say after normalisation. Convex means the two weights alpha and 1 - alpha are not negative and add up to 1.
symbols.phi (normaliser): A monotone function that rescales a score so that the two retrievers speak on a similar scale. Monotone means it never changes the order inside one retriever; it only changes the distance between scores.
symbols.m_q and M_q: The smallest and the largest score of one retriever over the candidate set of query q. They are recomputed for every query, so min-max depends on which documents happen to be in the set.
symbols.inf f: The theoretical minimum of the scoring function (the lowest value it can ever give): 0 for BM25, -1 for cosine. The paper uses it instead of m_q in the TM2C2 variant, which removes one data-dependent number.
symbols.phi_z: The z-score option: subtract the mean of the scores and divide by their standard deviation, both taken over the candidate set of the query.

units.inputs: For one query: a candidate set (the union of the top-k of the lexical and the dense retriever), a lexical and a dense score for every candidate (a missing one must be computed or filled), the normaliser, and alpha.
units.range: After min-max both inputs lie in [0,1], so the fused score lies in [0,1]. With theoretical-minimum normalisation the values stay in [0,1] but the lowest candidate need not reach 0. Only the order matters for ranking.

worked_example.setup: Invented toy inputs, computed by a local script (not published) Five candidates, BM25 and cosine scores as listed in step 1, alpha = 0.5.
steps: Toy inputs (invented): five candidates A-E in the union of both retrievers. BM25 scores {'A': 12.4, 'B': 9.1, 'C': 3.2, 'D': 0.0, 'E': 6.0}; cosine scores {'A': 0.41, 'B': 0.78, 'C': 0.83, 'D': 0.55, 'E': 0.62}. alpha = 0.5.

Without normalisation, 0.5*cos + 0.5*BM25 gives {'A': 6.405, 'B': 4.94, 'C': 2.015, 'D': 0.275, 'E': 3.31} and ranking ['A', 'B', 'E', 'C', 'D']. BM25 spans 0-12.4 and cosine spans 0.41-0.83, so BM25 decides almost alone: the semantic score barely matters.

Theoretical-minimum variant (paper Eq. 4, TM2C2): the minimum is replaced by the lowest possible value, 0 for BM25 and -1 for cosine. Scores {'A': 0.885, 'B': 0.853, 'C': 0.629, 'D': 0.423, 'E': 0.685}; ranking ['A', 'B', 'E', 'C', 'D'].

Sweeping alpha with min-max: alpha=0: ABECD; alpha=0.25: BAECD; alpha=0.5: BCAED; alpha=0.75: BCEAD (A and D tie at 0.25; ties broken alphabetically); alpha=1.0: CBEDA. alpha = 0 is pure BM25, alpha = 1 is pure dense.

blind_spots: Min-max uses the minimum and maximum of the current candidate set, so one outlier (a single very high BM25 score) squeezes all other documents together, and the same document can get a different normalised score for another candidate set.

alpha has to be tuned for the domain. The paper reports that tuning needs only a small set of labelled queries, but a value tuned on one dataset is not guaranteed to transfer (the paper's out-of-domain claim is about its own datasets).
A document found by only one retriever has no score from the other; it must be scored or given a default, and the default (0, the minimum, the mean) changes the ranking.
Scores that are nearly equal for all candidates (variance close to zero) make min-max and z-score unstable; the paper skips this case and does not analyse it.
Scores are only comparable inside one query; normalised scores are not a calibrated probability of relevance.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use convex fusion when you can afford a small labelled set to tune alpha and want the score distances to count. Use Reciprocal Rank Fusion (see RRF) when you have no labels or cannot see raw scores; it uses ranks only. Bruch et al. report that convex combination beat RRF on their in-domain and out-of-domain tests, and that RRF was sensitive to its parameters; that is their finding on their datasets, not a universal rule.

source.cite: Bruch, S., Gai, S. & Ingber, A. (2022/2023) An Analysis of Fusion Functions for Hybrid Retrieval. arXiv:2210.11934 (ACM TOIS). Read in the arXiv PDF: the convex form (Sec. 4), min-max Eq. 2, general form Eq. 3, theoretical-minimum Eq. 4, z-score Eq. 5, the TM2C2 / M2C2 naming and the abstract's claims.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in arXiv:2210.11934): the formulas for convex combination, min-max, theoretical-minimum and z-score normalisation, and the abstract's findings. Not opened: the venue version (ACM TOIS); the arXiv v2 text was used. The toy scores are invented; the numbers are computed by the script named above. 'Convex' wording follows the paper. Our statement that dense scores lie in [-1,1] holds for cosine only. Correction 2026-10-08 (demo build): at alpha=0.75 A and D tie exactly (0.25 each) under min-max; earlier text listed D before A from floating-point noise. superseded: 'alpha=0.75: BCEDA'.

units.name: Reranker: cross-encoder
units.question: How does reading query and passage together improve the order?

symbols.q: The query text, fed to BERT as sentence A (cut to at most 64 tokens in the paper).
symbols.d_i: One candidate passage, fed as sentence B. The whole input (query, passage, separators) is cut to 512 tokens.
symbols.[SEP], [CLS]: Special tokens. [SEP] separates query from passage. [CLS] is a summary position at the start; its final vector h is the model's reading of the whole pair.
symbols.h_[CLS](q [SEP] d_i): The vector BERT builds for the pair. Because query and passage sit in one input, every query word can attend to every passage word, so the model sees interactions a separate embedding cannot.
symbols.w: The weights of one extra linear layer on top of h. It turns the vector into one number (a logit).
symbols.sigma: The sigmoid function 1/(1+e^-x). It squeezes the logit into a probability between 0 and 1.
symbols.s_i: The relevance probability of passage i. Each passage is scored alone and independently; the final list is the passages sorted by s_i.
symbols.J_pos, J_neg: The sets of relevant and non-relevant passages among the top 1,000 returned by BM25 in training.
symbols.L: The cross-entropy training loss. A relevant passage with a small s adds a large -log s; a non-relevant passage with a large s adds a large -log(1-s). Training pushes s up for relevant and down for non-relevant passages.

units.inputs: A query and a short list of candidate passages from a first-stage retriever (BM25, dense, or hybrid), plus a fine-tuned cross-encoder model. The paper re-ranks the top 1,000 BM25 passages.
units.range: Each score is a probability in (0,1); only the order of scores for one query is used. Scores from different queries are not meant to be compared.

worked_example.setup: Invented toy numbers, computed by a local script (not published) No neural network was run; the logits are made up to show the mechanics. The pair-count and cost lines are plain arithmetic.
steps: Toy inputs (invented, not from a trained model): the first-stage retriever (for example BM25) returned five candidates p1..p5 in this order. Labels (1 = relevant) are p3 and p5. The cross-encoder logits for the pairs (query, passage) are p1 -2.1, p2 0.4, p3 2.6, p4 -0.7, p5 1.1.

Score each pair independently with the sigmoid s = 1/(1+exp(-logit)) (Nogueira & Cho feed [CLS] query [SEP] passage through BERT and apply one layer to get a probability): p1 0.1091, p2 0.5987, p3 0.9309, p4 0.3318, p5 0.7503.

Rank by s: ['p3', 'p5', 'p2', 'p4', 'p1']. First-stage order was ['p1', 'p2', 'p3', 'p4', 'p5']. The first relevant passage moves from rank 3 to rank 1: reciprocal rank 0.3333 -> 1.0 for this one query.
Training loss, Eq. 1 of the paper, on these five toy pairs: L = -sum over relevant log(s) - sum over non-relevant log(1-s) = 1.7907.

Cost (computed): a bi-encoder embeds each of M = 1,000,000 passages once, offline, then a query costs 1 encoder pass plus a nearest-neighbour search. A cross-encoder needs one full transformer pass per (query, passage) pair: scoring all 1,000,000 would be 1,000,000 passes per query; re-ranking only the top K = 100 is 100 passes. Reimers & Gurevych give the same logic for pairs: 10,000 sentences have 49,995,000 pairs (computed: n(n-1)/2), reported as about 65 hours with BERT.

blind_spots: Cost: one transformer pass per candidate and per query, no pre-computation. It can only re-rank a short list (tens to about a thousand), never the whole corpus.
Recall ceiling: the re-ranker cannot return a passage the first stage missed. If the relevant passage is not in the candidate list, re-ranking cannot help.
The input is cut to 512 tokens in the cited model; evidence beyond the cut is invisible, so long passages or documents need chunking.
Scores are trained on one domain (MS MARCO in the paper); how well they transfer to another domain is not shown by the cited sources (unverified here).
The probability s is not calibrated across queries; a fixed threshold such as 0.5 is not reliable.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use a cross-encoder as the second stage after a cheap retriever, when top-k order matters and you can pay K model passes per query. A bi-encoder (see Vector Similarity, Embeddings) is the right first stage because passages are embedded once. ColBERT-style late interaction sits between them: more token-level detail than a bi-encoder, cheaper than a full cross-encoder.

source.cite: Nogueira, R. & Cho, K. (2019) Passage Re-ranking with BERT. arXiv:1901.04085: method, input format, 512/64-token limits and the cross-entropy loss (Eq. 1) read in the arXiv PDF. Reimers, N. & Gurevych, I. (2019) Sentence-BERT. arXiv:1908.10084: the 10,000-sentence, 65-hour cross-encoder cost figure read in the abstract/introduction. The sigmoid form and the cost arithmetic for the toy are ours.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in the PDFs): the pair input, [CLS] to a single layer to a probability, ranking by that probability, the loss Eq. 1, the 64/512 token limits, BM25 top-1,000 candidates (Nogueira & Cho); the 65-hour / 10,000 sentences cost statement (Reimers & Gurevych). The explicit sigmoid is our reading of 'probability from a single layer'; the paper does not print the activation (unverified). The toy logits are invented. The paper's MS MARCO headline result (27% relative MRR@10 gain over the previous state of the art) is quoted from the abstract, not reproduced.
units.viz_why: A candidate table with logits and a bar chart of model passes; no spatial structure.

units.name: Reranker: ColBERT MaxSim (late interaction)
units.question: How do token-level vectors give a richer match than one vector?

symbols.q, d: The query and one document (or chunk). ColBERT scores one (q, d) pair at a time.
symbols.E_q: The query turned into a bag of vectors: one vector per query token (the paper pads short queries with [mask] tokens up to a fixed length N_q). Think of it as a matrix with one row per query token.
symbols.E_d: The document turned into a bag of vectors: one vector per document token (punctuation vectors are filtered out). A matrix with one row per document token. Documents are encoded offline, before any query arrives.
symbols.E_{q_i}: The vector of the i-th query token. It is contextual: it depends on the other words of the query.
symbols.E_{d_j}: The vector of the j-th document token, also contextual.
symbols.|E_q|, |E_d|: How many vectors are in each bag (the number of query tokens, the number of document tokens). The two bags can have different sizes.
symbols.E_{q_i} . E_{d_j}^T (dot product): Multiply the two vectors position by position and add. Because every vector is scaled to length 1, this equals the cosine similarity: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated, -1 = opposite. It is one cell of the similarity matrix (row i, column j).
symbols.max over j: For one query token, look along its whole row of the similarity matrix and keep only the best match among all document tokens. That is the MaxSim operator: each query token finds its best partner in the document.
symbols.sum over i: Add up the row maxima of all query tokens. A query token that finds no good partner adds a low number, so every query token must be covered for a high score.
symbols.S_{q,d}: The final relevance score of document d for query q: a sum of one best-match cosine per query token. It is at most |E_q| (every query token has a perfect partner with cosine 1) and at least -|E_q|.

units.inputs: E_q: m-dimensional unit vectors, one per query token; E_d: m-dimensional unit vectors, one per document token (both made by the same BERT-based encoder; in the paper m is much smaller than BERT's hidden size). In the demo the encoder is replaced by an editable table of token-to-token cosine similarities.
units.range: Each cell is a cosine in [-1, 1]. Each row maximum is in [-1, 1]. The score S is in [-|E_q|, |E_q|]; in practice close to 0 to |E_q| for relevant documents. It is NOT normalised by query length, so it only ranks documents for ONE query; scores of different queries are not comparable.

worked_example.setup: Toy example, invented for teaching. 2-D unit token vectors given by their angle. Query has 3 tokens at 0, 60, 120 degrees. Document D1 has 5 tokens at 0, 60, 120, 240, 300 degrees (one exact partner for every query token, plus two tokens pointing the other way). Document D2 has 3 tokens at 50, 60, 70 degrees (all near the middle of the query, none exact). The similarity tables below are the cosines of the angle differences rounded to 2 decimals (that table is the editable input of the demo). For the single-vector contrast, each token bag is averaged into one vector and compared with cosine.
steps: D1 row maxima: 1.00, 1.00, 1.00. MaxSim S(q, D1) = 1.00 + 1.00 + 1.00 = 3.00 (the maximum possible for 3 query tokens).
MaxSim ranks D1 (3.00) above D2 (2.28): D1 has an exact partner for every query token.

Single-vector contrast: the mean of the query tokens points at 60 degrees. The mean of D2's tokens also points at 60 degrees: cosine = 1.00. The mean of D1's five tokens points at 0 degrees (the opposite tokens cancel the topic): cosine = 0.50. One averaged vector ranks D2 (1.00) above D1 (0.50), the opposite order.

blind_spots: Cost: a document is many vectors, not one. Storage and search grow with the number of tokens (the paper reports the space footprint as a main cost; ColBERTv2 compresses it, not re-checked here). It is the reason MaxSim is used as a reranker or with a token-level index, not as a flat scan of everything.
Scores are not normalised: S is a sum over query tokens, so longer queries give larger scores. Compare documents for the same query only, never across queries.

Each query token takes its best match independently, so two query tokens can use the SAME document token, and word order and word-to-word alignment are ignored (the model only sees contextual vectors).

Every query token counts equally: a stop word that matches well adds as much as a rare content word (the paper pads queries with [mask] tokens that also take part in the sum; their effect was measured in the paper's ablation, not re-checked here).
Quality depends on the encoder: contextual token vectors from a model not trained for late interaction are not guaranteed to give meaningful MaxSim scores (unverified).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use MaxSim when one vector per chunk loses detail: long chunks with several topics, queries with several distinct terms that must all be covered, or rare-term matching you would otherwise need BM25 for. It sits between a bi-encoder (one vector per text, cheap, see vector_similarity) and a cross-encoder (reads query and document together, most accurate, slowest): documents are encoded offline like a bi-encoder, but the query-document match is token level. Neighbours: vector_similarity is the single-vector baseline (and MaxSim reuses its cosine per token pair); BM25 matches exact words only; a cross-encoder reranker usually costs more per pair; RRF can fuse a MaxSim ranking with other rankings.

source.cite: Khattab & Zaharia (2020) ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT, SIGIR 2020, section 3.3 Late Interaction, Equation 3 (S_{q,d} := sum over i in [|E_q|] of max over j in [|E_d|] of E_{q_i} . E_{d_j}^T); section 3.2 (embeddings L2-normalised so the dot product equals cosine).

units.notes: Evidenced: Equation 3 (sum of row-wise max of dot products), the statement that embeddings are L2-normalised so dot product equals cosine, the query [mask] padding to N_q, document punctuation filtering, and that squared L2 is also evaluated, all read in the arXiv PDF (text extracted with markitdown; the equation was garbled by the extractor but its structure sum_i max_j E_qi . E_dj^T is unambiguous together with the prose 'maximum cosine similarity of each v in E_q with vectors in E_d and combine the outputs via summation'). Computed in code: all matrices, row maxima, sums and cosines. Ours (toy): 2-D vectors at chosen angles, the 3-token query, and the mean-pooling single-vector baseline (real single-vector models may use CLS or another pooling, so the contrast shows the idea, not a specific model). Not checked: ColBERTv2 compression claims; effect of [mask] tokens beyond the paper's text.

units.name: Maximal Marginal Relevance (diversity)
units.question: How do we pick results that are relevant and not redundant?

symbols.D_i: One candidate chunk that has not been picked yet. It comes from R minus S.
symbols.Q: The query (or user profile). In RAG: the question, as a vector.
symbols.R: The ranked list the first-stage retriever returned for Q (the candidate pool). MMR only re-orders and cuts this list; it finds nothing new.
symbols.S: The set of chunks already picked. It starts empty and grows by one chunk per step.
symbols.R\\S: R without S: the candidates still waiting. Each step picks exactly one of them.
symbols.Sim_1(D_i, Q): Relevance: how similar the candidate is to the query. In the toy example this is cosine similarity; the paper only says it is the similarity metric used for relevance ranking.
symbols.Sim_2(D_i, D_j): Redundancy: how similar two chunks are to each other. It can be the same metric as Sim_1 or a different one (the paper says so). Here: cosine.
symbols.max over D_j in S: Take the single most similar chunk among the picks so far. One close copy is enough to count the candidate as redundant.
symbols.lambda: The dial between 0 and 1. lambda = 1 means only relevance (the plain ranked list). lambda = 0 means only novelty. The paper suggests a small lambda (about 0.3) to explore the area around the query, and a larger one (about 0.7) to focus.
symbols.1 - lambda: The weight of the redundancy penalty. It grows as lambda shrinks.
symbols.arg max: Choose the candidate with the largest value in the brackets. Do this k times; each pick joins S.
symbols.MMR: The chosen chunk of this step. The bracket value is its marginal-relevance score; it can be negative and has no meaning outside one query.

units.inputs: Query vector Q, the candidate list R (here 6 chunks as unit vectors at angles 10, 17, 24, 55, -40, 78 degrees; Q at 0 degrees), lambda in [0,1] (default 0.4), and k, how many chunks to keep (default 3).
units.range: With cosine the bracket lies between -(1-lambda) and lambda (relevance at most 1, redundancy at most 1). It can be negative. Only the order of the values inside one step matters; the value is not a probability and not comparable between queries.
units.higher_is_better: n/a (a selection rule, not a quality score; at each step the largest bracket value wins)

worked_example.setup: Six toy chunks A-F as unit vectors in 2-D at angles 10, 17, 24, 55, -40 and 78 degrees; the query Q is at 0 degrees. Sim_1 = Sim_2 = cosine. Relevance to Q: A 0.985, B 0.956, C 0.914, D 0.574, E 0.766, F 0.208. A, B, C sit close together (near-copies). lambda = 0.4, k = 3. Toy numbers invented for teaching, not from a real index.
steps: lambda = 1 (plain relevance): picks A, B, C: three near-copies of one idea.
Step 1: S is empty, so the redundancy term is 0 (our convention; the paper does not state it). Score = 0.4 x relevance, so A wins with 0.394.

Step 2, S = {A}. Candidate B: relevance 0.956, similarity to A 0.993, score 0.4 x 0.956 - 0.6 x 0.993 = -0.213. Candidate E: relevance 0.766, similarity to A 0.643, score -0.079. E wins (the others: C -0.217, D -0.195, F -0.142).
Step 3, S = {A, E}: the best remaining is F with score -0.142. Even F, far from the query (relevance 0.208), beats B and C because they are copies of A.
Result at lambda 0.4: A, E, F. Sweep over lambda -> 1: A B C; 0.7: A B E; 0.5: A E B; 0.4: A E F; 0: A F E.

blind_spots: lambda = 1 returns the plain relevance list: here A, B, C, three near-duplicates (cosine between A and B is 0.993). MMR with lambda near 1 does almost nothing.
lambda = 0 ignores the query: the first pick is a tie among all candidates (here the lowest index wins), and later picks are the most spread-out chunks, which can be off-topic.
Greedy: each pick is the best given the earlier picks, so the final set is not guaranteed to be the best set of k (inferred from the algorithm, not tested against an exact search here).
Similarity is only as good as the vectors: if the embedding calls two different facts similar, MMR drops one of them; if it calls two paraphrases different, MMR keeps both (inferred).
lambda is hand-tuned and query-dependent; the paper gives only the suggestions 0.3 (explore) and 0.7 (focus), from a small pilot with five users.
One far-away chunk is enough to look novel: with lambda 0.4 the weak chunk F (relevance 0.208) is picked as third. Add a relevance floor if weak chunks are not allowed.
MMR needs the candidate pool R from a first stage; if the pool lacks diverse chunks, MMR cannot create them.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use MMR after retrieval (vector, BM25 or fused list) when the top-k contains near-duplicates, e.g. overlapping chunks or many copies of one fact, and you want a short, varied context. Use plain top-k when the answer is a single fact and duplicates are harmless. Use RRF (rrf_fusion) to merge lists, MMR to diversify one list; they combine: fuse, then MMR. Use a cross-encoder or ColBERT reranker when order accuracy matters more than variety. Neighbours: vector_similarity gives Sim; clustering or deduplication removes exact copies before MMR.

source.cite: Carbonell, J., Goldstein, J. (1998) The Use of MMR, Diversity-Based Reranking for Reordering Documents and Producing Summaries. SIGIR 98, pp. 335-336.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in the paper, 2-page SIGIR 98 PDF, formula checked on the rendered page 1): MMR = Arg max over D_i in R\S of [lambda Sim_1(D_i,Q) - (1-lambda) max over D_j in S Sim_2(D_i,D_j)]; R = IR(C,Q,theta); S = already selected; Sim_2 may equal Sim_1; lambda = 1 gives the standard relevance-ranked list, lambda = 0 a maximal-diversity ranking; lambda = .3 to explore and .7 to focus. Computed in code (Python and node): every score, pick and sweep in the worked example. Ours: the 2-D toy vectors, cosine as both Sim, the chunk names, the convention that the first pick has redundancy 0 (the paper does not say what max over an empty S is). Elasticsearch Labs blog confirms the same formula in RAG vocabulary (read). Not checked: how LangChain (lambda_mult), Elasticsearch and vector stores implement it exactly (unverified; some use a fetch_k pool).

units.name: Query translation: multi-query and RAG-Fusion
units.question: How do several rewrites of the question raise recall?

symbols.q_1 ... q_n: The rewrites: new search queries that an LLM writes from the original question, each looking at it from another angle (RAG-Fusion's own example turns 'Tell me about MEMs microphones' into 'What are the advantages of using MEMs microphones?').
symbols.LLM(q_0): One call to a language model with the instruction to write n related queries. The output is not fixed: another call can give different rewrites.
symbols.rank_i(d): The position (1 = best) of document d in the result list of query i, found by vector search. If d is not in that list it adds nothing.
symbols.k: A smoothing constant. A big k makes the gap between rank 1 and rank 2 small; a small k makes top ranks count much more. Cormack et al. fixed k = 60 in a pilot study and found it near-optimal on their data; RAG-Fusion's paper only calls it a smoothing factor.
symbols.1/(k + rank): The vote a list gives to a document. Top ranks give bigger votes; the votes of all lists are added.
symbols.RRF(d): The fused score of document d. Documents are sorted by it, and the top ones go to the LLM that writes the answer.

units.inputs: The original query, a number n of rewrites to generate, a retriever that returns a ranked list per query, the constant k, and how many fused documents to keep.
units.range: Each score is positive and at most (n+1)/(k+1). For k = 60 and 4 lists the maximum is 4/61 = 0.0656. Only the order matters.

worked_example.setup: Invented toy lists, computed by a local script (not published) No LLM or retriever was run.
steps: Toy inputs (invented): the original question q0 and three LLM rewrites each retrieve a ranked list of 4 documents: {'q0 (original)': ['d1', 'd2', 'd3', 'd4'], 'q1 (rewrite 1)': ['d2', 'd5', 'd1', 'd6'], 'q2 (rewrite 2)': ['d5', 'd2', 'd7', 'd3'], 'q3 (rewrite 3)': ['d8', 'd2', 'd5', 'd1']}.
RAG-Fusion (Rackauckas 2024, Eq. 1): for each document, add 1/(rank + k) for every list that contains it. We use k = 60, the value Cormack et al. fixed in a pilot study.
Fused ranking (k = 60): ['d2', 'd5', 'd1', 'd3', 'd8', 'd7', 'd4', 'd6']. d2 is in all four lists and wins; d5 is in three; d1 is in three but ranks worse in them.
Effect of k (computed): with k = 1 the ranking is ['d2', 'd5', 'd1', 'd8', 'd3', 'd7', 'd4', 'd6']. Small k lets a rank-1 hit dominate; large k flattens the difference between ranks.

Recall check against an invented relevant set ['d2', 'd5', 'd8']: the original query's top 4 ['d1', 'd2', 'd3', 'd4'] contains 1 of 3 (recall 0.333); the fused top 4 ['d2', 'd5', 'd1', 'd3'] contains 2 of 3 (recall 0.667).

blind_spots: Query drift: rewrites can move away from what the user asked. The RAG-Fusion paper itself reports that some answers strayed off topic when the generated queries were not strictly related to the original query.
Cost and delay: one extra LLM call plus n retrievals per question. The paper reports the query-generation call took up to about 5 seconds in its test.
RRF uses ranks only and throws away score gaps, so a document that is a clear winner in one list but missing from others can lose to a mediocre document that appears everywhere.
The paper's evidence is a small, manual evaluation on one company chatbot, not a benchmark; it does not prove a recall gain in general. Our recall numbers are on invented data.
The rewrites are random; two runs can give two different fused lists.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use multi-query + RRF when one phrasing of the question often misses the right passages and a few extra seconds are acceptable. HyDE (see HyDE) rewrites into a fake answer instead of more questions. Decomposition splits a multi-part question into different sub-questions; multi-query asks the same question in other words. For fusing lexical and dense scores of the same query, see RRF Fusion and Convex Fusion.

source.cite: Rackauckas, Z. (2024) RAG-Fusion: a New Take on Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2402.03367 (Int. J. NLP & Applications): pipeline, Eq. 1, the example rewrites, the query-drift observation and the timing note read in the arXiv PDF. Cormack, G., Clarke, C. & Buettcher, S. (2009) Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learning methods. SIGIR 2009: the sum of 1/(k+rank) and k = 60 'fixed during a pilot investigation' read in the author-hosted PDF.

units.notes: Evidenced (read): RAG-Fusion pipeline (generate queries, vector search per query, RRF, send to LLM), Eq. 1 and the drift and timing observations; Cormack et al.'s formula and k = 60. Not opened: RAG-Fusion's published journal version (the arXiv version was used). Note the arXiv Eq. 1 is printed for a single list ('accumulated with previous scores'); the sum over lists is stated in prose and in Cormack. The relevant set and all lists are invented.
units.viz_why: Ranked lists and stacked score bars; fusion is arithmetic on ranks.

units.name: Query translation: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)
units.question: How does a hypothetical answer retrieve better than the question?
units.formula_latex: \hat v_q=\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^{N} f(\hat d_k),\quad \hat d_k\sim g(q,\mathrm{INST})\qquad \text{optionally}\quad \hat v_q=\frac1{N+1}\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{N} f(\hat d_k)+f(q)\Big]\qquad \mathrm{score}(d)=\hat v_q\cdot f(d)

symbols.INST: A fixed instruction given to the language model, for example 'write a paragraph that answers the question'.
symbols.g(q, INST): The instruction-following language model. Each call (with sampling, so the answers differ) writes one short fake document that answers q.
symbols.d_hat_k: The k-th hypothetical document the language model wrote. It may be wrong: the paper says it 'is not real' and 'is likely to be ungrounded factually'. It only has to look like a relevant answer.
symbols.N: How many hypothetical documents are sampled. More samples average out the noise of any single answer.
symbols.f(.): The document encoder: the same embedding model that embedded the real chunks (in the paper an unsupervised contrastive encoder, Contriever). It turns text into a vector and drops fine details, which is why invented specifics do little harm.
symbols.f(d_hat_k): The embedding (a list of numbers, here 2 in the teaching picture) of the k-th fake document.
symbols.v_hat_q: The search vector: the average of the N fake-document embeddings (and, in the second form, of the question embedding as one more vote). It replaces the question's own embedding.
symbols.f(q): The embedding of the question itself. The second formula adds it as one more hypothesis, with weight 1/(N+1) like the others.
symbols.score(d): The inner product of the search vector with the embedding of a real chunk d. The chunk with the highest score is retrieved. On chunk vectors of length 1 this ranks exactly like cosine similarity to v_hat_q.

units.inputs: q: question; N hypothetical documents written by a language model (here given as 2-D embedding vectors); real chunk embeddings (2-D toy); a switch for adding f(q) to the average.
units.range: The score is an unbounded inner product; on unit chunk vectors it lies in [-|v|, |v|].

worked_example.setup: Toy 2-D embeddings (invented for teaching, not from a real model). Question q = (0.2, 0.98). Real chunks (length about 1): G (gold, answers the question) = (0.94, 0.34); X = (0.34, 0.94), shares the question's words but does not answer it; Y = (0.64, 0.77); Z = (-0.5, 0.87), off topic. The language model writes N = 3 hypothetical answers; their embeddings are h1 = (0.82, 0.57), h2 = (0.97, 0.26), h3 = (0.77, 0.64). Score = inner product.
steps: Question as the search vector: scores G 0.521, X 0.989, Y 0.883, Z 0.753. The gold chunk G is ranked 4th of 4 (X, Y, Z are all ahead).
Average the three hypothetical embeddings: v_hat = ((0.82+0.97+0.77)/3, (0.57+0.26+0.64)/3) = (0.853, 0.490).
Score the real chunks with v_hat: G 0.969, Y 0.923, X 0.751, Z -0.0004 (about 0). The gold chunk G is now ranked 1st.
Why: the question is short and sits near X (similar words); the hypothetical answers are written like a document, so their average lies near the answer chunks.

blind_spots: If the language model is confidently wrong (it does not know the domain, or the question needs private facts), all hypothetical documents land in the wrong region and retrieval follows them there. In the demo's break-it preset the question itself (0.85, 0.53) already ranks the gold chunk 1st, all three fake answers point at chunk Z, and the gold chunk drops from 1st to 4th (computed). Adding f(q) to the average (second formula) does not rescue it: still 4th.
HyDE assumes the answer distribution is single-peaked ('the query is not ambiguous' in the paper); an ambiguous question is averaged into a vector between its meanings that matches neither well.

The encoder removes fine details, so a wrong number or name inside a fake document usually changes little, but it also means HyDE cannot add exact-term matching (IDs, error codes): a fake document does not know your real identifiers.

Cost and latency: one (or N) language-model calls before every search, and the model's own knowledge decides the quality. Gains in the paper were measured with a large instruction-tuned LM (InstructGPT) and Contriever; they are not guaranteed for other pairs (not re-measured here).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use HyDE when questions are short or phrased unlike the documents and the language model knows the topic (zero-shot, no relevance labels). Prefer multi-query or RAG-Fusion when you want several rewordings of the same question rather than an answer; step-back or decomposition when the question is too specific or has several parts; plain vector or BM25 search when the question already uses the documents' words or contains exact identifiers. Avoid it when the model knows nothing about the topic (private data): it will hallucinate in the wrong place.

source.cite: Gao, Ma, Lin, Callan (2022) Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE), arXiv 2212.10496, Section 3 equations 5-8.

units.notes: Evidenced: equations 5-8 (expectation of f(g(q,INST)), estimate as the mean of N sampled document embeddings, the (N+1) variant that includes f(q), inner product against document vectors) and the statements 'can and is likely to be ungrounded factually', 'extra details are filtered and left out', 'query is not ambiguous' were read in the arXiv PDF text (Section 3). Paper results read: Table 1 TREC DL19 ndcg@10 Contriever 44.5 vs HyDE 61.3. Not found in the text we extracted: the exact N used in experiments (unverified). All vectors, chunks and texts in the worked example are invented 2-D toys; real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions and the 2-D picture cannot show that. The paper's encoder is not length-normalised; we use unit-length chunks so that inner product equals cosine ranking. Query-translation backbone from the human's Attachments/RAG-Parts.md ('translate question to a form that is better suited for a retriever: re-phrase, break-down, abstract, convert to hypothetical doc; Multi-Query, RAG Fusion, Decomposition, Step-Back, HyDE').

units.name: Query translation: step-back prompting
units.question: How does a more general question help retrieval?

symbols.q: The original question, full of specific details (a name, a date, a number). Details can hide the general idea the answer depends on.
symbols.q': The step-back question: a more general question about the higher-level concept or principle behind q (for example 'What was Estella Leopold's education history?' for a question about one date range). The LLM writes it after seeing a few examples (few-shot).
symbols.LLM_few-shot: A language model prompted with a handful of example pairs (question, step-back question). The paper says the step-back question is task-specific, so the examples are written per task.
symbols.Retrieve(q'): Search with the general question and get relevant facts. The paper does this with retrieval augmentation for knowledge questions (TimeQA); for physics and chemistry the step back recalls principles with the LLM itself, with no retriever.
symbols.C: The retrieved context: facts about the high-level concept or principle.
symbols.a = LLM(q | C): The final answer: the model reasons about the original question q, grounded on C. The paper calls this abstraction-grounded reasoning.

units.inputs: The original question, a few-shot prompt that shows how to step back for this kind of task, a retriever and corpus (or the LLM's own knowledge), and a prompt for the final answer.
units.range: No score is defined by the method. In the paper the outcome is task accuracy (0-100%): for example PaLM-2L on TimeQA 41.5% baseline, 57.4% with plain RAG, 68.7% with Step-Back + RAG.

worked_example.setup: Invented toy corpus and a hand-written step-back question; scoring is word-count cosine (our simplification, not the paper's retriever). Computed by a local script (not published) No LLM was run.
steps: Toy inputs (invented, loosely modelled on the paper's Estella Leopold example): five passages P1..P5; original question q0 = 'Estella Leopold went to which school between Aug 1954 and Nov 1954?'; step-back question = 'What was Estella Leopold's education history?'. In the paper the LLM writes the step-back question from few-shot examples; here we wrote it by hand.

Scoring (our simplification, not the paper's retriever): cosine similarity of word-count vectors after removing a small stop-word list. Content words of q0: ['estella', 'leopold', 'school', 'aug', '1954', 'nov', '1954']; of the step-back question: ['estella', 'leopold', 'education', 'history'].

Reading the result: the passage that holds the answer (P1, the education timeline) is rank 3 for the original question and rank 2 for the step-back question. The specific question's date words ('1954') pull in P3, which mentions 1954 but not her education.

Reasoning step (paper): the LLM gets the retrieved facts as context and then answers the original question (here: the PhD at Yale ran to 1955, so Aug-Nov 1954 falls inside it). We did not run an LLM; this last sentence repeats the logic of the paper's Figure 2.

blind_spots: The step-back question is written by an LLM and can be wrong or too vague; then the retrieved facts are about the wrong thing. The paper's error analysis finds the reasoning step, not the abstraction step, is the main bottleneck, but it also lists context loss and step-back errors.
It adds one extra LLM call and, for knowledge tasks, a second retrieval, so cost and delay go up.
A question that is already general gains nothing; a step back that is too general retrieves broad passages that do not contain the needed detail.
The reported gains are for PaLM-2L, GPT-4 and Llama2-70B on selected tasks (STEM, TimeQA, MuSiQue, StrategyQA); the paper does not show the gain in an ordinary enterprise RAG corpus (unverified).
Our toy ranking uses word overlap, which shows the idea of vocabulary mismatch but is not how a dense retriever behaves.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use step-back when the question is packed with specifics and the answer depends on a general concept or timeline that the specific wording does not retrieve. Multi-query rewrites the same question several ways; decomposition splits it into parts; HyDE writes a fake answer. Step-back goes up in generality instead. It can be combined with RAG-Fusion or reranking.

source.cite: Zheng, H. S., Mishra, S., Chen, X., Cheng, H.-T., Chi, E. H., Le, Q. V. & Zhou, D. (2023/2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models. arXiv:2310.06117 (ICLR 2024). Read in the arXiv PDF: the two steps (abstraction, reasoning), the Estella Leopold example, the use of step-back with RAG on TimeQA, and the TimeQA accuracies 41.5 / 57.4 / 68.7. The three-line formula is our compact notation for the two steps.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in arXiv:2310.06117): the two-step procedure, the role of retrieval in the knowledge tasks, the example, and the TimeQA numbers. The formula line is our notation, not printed in the paper. The toy corpus, the hand-written step-back question and the word-count cosine are invented/simplified; their numbers are computed by the script named above. Not opened: appendix prompts (Table 14) beyond a grep.
units.viz_why: Two queries scored against a passage list as bars; vocabulary matching, not geometry.

units.name: Query translation: decomposition
units.question: How do sub-questions answer a multi-part question?
units.formula_latex: q \;\to\; (q_1,q_2,\dots,q_m),\quad a_i=\mathrm{Answer}(q_i\,[a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}]),\quad a=a_m;\qquad \mathrm{gap}=\frac{P(\text{all sub-answers right}\wedge\text{composed wrong})}{P(\text{all sub-answers right})}

symbols.q: The original multi-part question, for example a question that needs a person, then that person's birthplace, then a date.
symbols.q_1 ... q_m: The sub-questions. In self-ask each one starts with 'Follow up:' and the model asks them one at a time. m is the number of hops.
symbols.a_i: The answer to sub-question i. In the paper it is written as 'Intermediate answer:' and can come from the model's own memory or from a search engine.
symbols.[a_1..a_(i-1)]: The earlier answers are copied into later sub-questions (sub-question 2 is 'Where was Mara Voss born?', not 'Where was the director born?'). This is why the steps are called sequential.
symbols.Answer(.): One call to the language model or to a retriever plus reader for one small question.
symbols.a: The final answer, written after the last intermediate answer ('So the final answer is: ...').
symbols.gap (compositionality gap): Press et al.'s measure: among questions where the model gets every sub-question right, the share where it still gets the combined question wrong. A gap above 0 means knowing the facts is not enough to combine them.

units.inputs: A multi-part question, a prompt with a few worked examples of how to decompose (or a trained decomposer), an answering module for each sub-question (LLM, retriever + reader, or a search engine), and a stop rule.
units.range: No score for the method itself. The gap is a ratio between 0 and 1 (the paper quotes it as a percentage): 0 means composed questions are answered as well as their parts.

worked_example.setup: Invented toy question and 3-sentence knowledge base; invented counts for the gap line. Computed by a local script (not published) No LLM was run; the decomposition is written by hand in the self-ask format.
steps: Toy question (invented): 'When was the birthplace of the director of 'Harbor Lights' first documented?'. Toy knowledge base (invented, 3 sentences): ['Harbor Lights was directed by Mara Voss.', 'Mara Voss was born in Tallin.', 'Records first mention the city of Tallin in 1219.'].

Single retrieval with the whole question (word-overlap scoring, our simplification): overlap counts {"Who directed the film 'Harbor Lights'?": 2, 'Where was Mara Voss born?': 0, 'When was Tallin founded?': 1} (common words removed); the best single hit is the sentence for 'Who directed the film 'Harbor Lights'?', which does not contain the final answer 1219.

Decomposition (self-ask pattern from Press et al.): the model writes 'Are follow up questions needed here: Yes.' then one follow-up question at a time, each answered before the next is asked: Follow up: Who directed the film 'Harbor Lights'? -> Intermediate answer: Mara Voss | Follow up: Where was Mara Voss born? -> Intermediate answer: Tallin | Follow up: When was Tallin founded? -> Intermediate answer: 1219. Final line: 'So the final answer is: 1219'.
Retrieval calls: 3 small ones, each hits exactly the sentence it needs; the answer to hop 1 ('Mara Voss') is substituted into hop 2, and the answer to hop 2 ('Tallin') into hop 3. Number of hops = 3.

Compositionality gap (Press et al. define it as how often a model answers all sub-questions right but the composed question wrong). Invented counts: of 100 two-hop questions, 60 have both sub-answers right; of these, 36 also have the composed answer right. Gap = (60 - 36) / 60 = 0.40. Real values from the paper: 42.9% for ChatGPT and 23.0% for GPT-4 on its Compositional Celebrities set (the paper warns the GPT-4 figure may be contaminated).

blind_spots: Error propagation: if a_1 is wrong, every later sub-question is built on the wrong answer. Chains get less reliable as m grows.
A bad decomposition (missing a hop, or sub-questions that cannot be answered alone) fails silently; the model may sound confident.
More calls: m LLM calls plus m retrievals, so cost and delay grow with the number of hops. The sequence cannot be parallel when later questions need earlier answers.
Not every question is multi-hop. Splitting a single-fact question only adds noise and cost.

The paper shows the compositionality gap does not shrink with model size on its dataset; decomposition narrows it in the paper's tests, but results depend on the model, the dataset and prompt, and were not rerun by us.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use decomposition for questions that need several facts chained or combined (multi-hop QA). Multi-query asks the same question in other words; step-back asks a more general one; for corpus-wide questions, GraphRAG-style global search (see MS Local/Global) summarises communities instead. Self-ask (Press et al.) is sequential and uses the LLM or a search engine for sub-answers; Decomposed Prompting (Khot et al.) adds a library of modules (sub-task handlers, including a retriever) that a decomposer prompt calls, so sub-tasks can be solved by different prompts or symbolic code.

source.cite: Press, O., Zhang, M., Min, S., Schmidt, L., Smith, N. A. & Lewis, M. (2022/2023) Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models. arXiv:2210.03350 (Findings of EMNLP 2023): definition of the gap, 'Follow up:' / 'Intermediate answer:' format, gap not shrinking with scale, ChatGPT 42.9% and GPT-4 23.0% read in the arXiv PDF. Khot, T. et al. (2022/2023) Decomposed Prompting: A Modular Approach for Solving Complex Tasks. arXiv:2210.02406 (ICLR 2023): abstract and first page read; the module architecture is stated from the abstract and not studied in detail.

units.notes: Evidenced (read): the compositionality-gap definition and the quoted ChatGPT/GPT-4 percentages, the self-ask trace format (Press et al.); the idea of a modular decomposer (Khot et al., abstract). Not studied in depth: Khot et al.'s module library and its experiments. The formula line is our compact notation; the paper defines the gap in words. All toy counts and sentences are invented. The accuracy-product statement in demo_hint is simple probability assuming independent hops (our assumption, unverified for real systems).
units.viz_why: A step-by-step hop trace of questions and answers; a sequence, not a space.
