units.name: ANN index: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)
units.question: How does a layered graph find near neighbours without scanning everything?

symbols.l: The top layer of one node. Every node lives in layer 0; a lucky few also live in layer 1, fewer in layer 2, and so on. Think of layers as zoom levels of a map.
symbols.U: A random number between 0 and 1, drawn once when the node is inserted. It is the dice roll that decides the node's level.
symbols.ln(U), floor: ln(U) is negative for U < 1; the minus sign makes it positive. floor rounds it down to a whole layer number. Small U (rare) gives a high layer.
symbols.m_L: Level normalisation factor, a knob. It sets how quickly the number of nodes drops from one layer to the next. The paper finds m_L = 1/ln(M) is a good choice.
symbols.M: How many links each new node makes to its nearest neighbours in each layer (the paper's M; layer 0 may keep more, M_max0). Larger M: better recall, more memory, slower build.
symbols.P(level >= l) = M^-l: With m_L = 1/ln(M), the chance that a node reaches layer l or above is 1/M^l. So each layer holds about 1/M of the nodes of the layer below. Few nodes at the top = long, coarse jumps.
symbols.N: Number of vectors in the index. The number of layers grows like log_M(N), and a search walks a short path in each layer.
symbols.efConstruction, ef: Size of the candidate list kept during insertion (efConstruction) and during search (ef). Bigger ef = look at more candidates = higher recall, slower. ef = 1 means a pure greedy walk.
symbols.greedy step: At a node, look at its neighbours in this layer; if one is closer to the query than the current node, move there. Stop when no neighbour is closer. Then go down one layer from that node.

units.inputs: A set of N vectors with a distance function; build knobs M, M_max0, efConstruction and m_L; at query time a query vector, the number k of neighbours wanted, and ef.
units.range: Search returns approximate nearest neighbours: recall between 0 and 1 (1 = exactly the true k nearest). Query cost grows about logarithmically with N (the paper reports this empirically, with a heuristic argument), instead of linearly for brute force.

worked_example.setup: Part 1 (formula, computed): M = 16, N = 1,000,000. Part 2 (toy, our simplified implementation, invented data): 60 random 2-D points (seed 7), M = 4, links = 4 nearest per layer, greedy search with ef = 1, query q = (0.83, 0.21). The toy is not the full paper algorithm (no heuristic neighbour selection, no ef > 1 beam).
steps: Level draw (Algorithm 1, line 4 of the paper): level = floor(-ln(U) * mL), U uniform in (0,1), mL = 1/ln(M). For M = 16: mL = 0.3607. So P(level >= l) = M^-l: 1/16 = 0.0625 of nodes reach layer 1, 1/256 = 0.0039 reach layer 2.

Expected layer sizes for N = 1,000,000 nodes and M = 16 (computed): layer 0: 1,000,000, layer 1: 62,500, layer 2: 3,906, layer 3: 244, layer 4: 15. The number of layers is about log_M(N) = ln(1e6)/ln(16) = 4.98.

Toy build (our simplified code, invented data): N = 60 random 2-D points, seed 7, M = 4, mL = 1/ln(4) = 0.7213. Each node gets a drawn level. Nodes per layer from layer 0 up: [60, 14, 4, 2]. Each node is linked to its 4 nearest nodes inside every layer it belongs to (links made two-way).

Query q = (0.83, 0.21). Start at the entry point (a node on top layer 3). On each layer walk greedily: move to any neighbour that is closer to q, repeat until none is closer, then drop one layer with the same node. Walk (layer, node): [(3, 51), (2, 51), (1, 30), (0, 37)].
Result: the walk ends at node 37; the true nearest node (brute force) is node 37. The walk computed 15 distances to q, brute force needs 60.

blind_spots: Approximate: it can miss the true nearest neighbour. In our toy run the greedy walk found the true nearest node; with ef = 1 a walk can get stuck in a local minimum. Raise ef to trade speed for recall.
Memory heavy: every vector keeps its links in every layer it belongs to, on top of the vectors themselves, and the index is normally held in RAM.
Recall depends on M, efConstruction and ef; bad settings silently lower recall, and the quality has to be measured against brute force on a sample of queries.

Built for similarity search only: it cannot filter by metadata exactly (filtered search needs extra tricks and can lower recall) and deletions or updates are awkward (unverified for specific libraries).

In very high dimension or with clustered / duplicate data, graph quality can degrade (the paper discusses clustered data and the heuristic selection that addresses it; the extent for modern embeddings is unverified).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use HNSW when you have more than about 10^5 vectors and brute-force cosine scan is too slow. For small collections an exact scan (see Vector Similarity) is simpler and exact. IVF / product-quantisation indexes use less memory but usually need more tuning; HNSW is the common default in vector databases (this popularity claim is unverified here). HNSW only speeds up finding neighbours; it does not change what 'near' means (that is the vector similarity unit).

source.cite: Malkov, Y. A. & Yashunin, D. A. (2016/2018) Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs. arXiv:1603.09320 (published in IEEE TPAMI 2020). units.name: ANN index: IVF and product quantisation
units.question: How do clusters and compressed codes trade recall for speed and memory?

symbols.y: A database vector. x is the query vector.
symbols.q_c: The coarse quantizer: k-means with k' centroids (the paper uses 1,000 to 1,000,000). It maps a vector to its nearest coarse centroid, the 'cell' it lives in. Each cell has a list of its vectors: the inverted file (IVF).
symbols.y - q_c(y): The residual: the small offset of the vector from the centre of its cell. It has less energy than y, so it can be compressed more precisely.
symbols.q_p: The product quantizer. It cuts the residual into m equal sub-vectors u_1..u_m and replaces each by the nearest of k* centroids in its own small codebook. Only the m centroid indices are stored.
symbols.m: The number of sub-vectors (and sub-quantizers). More sub-vectors means a longer code and a better approximation. D must be divisible by m.
symbols.k*: The number of centroids per sub-quantizer (often 256 so that one index fits in one byte).
symbols.k = (k*)^m: The number of different vectors the product quantizer can represent: the product of the small codebooks. With m = 8 and k* = 256 that is 2^64 values, though only 8 x 256 centroids are stored.
symbols.m log2 k*: The code length in bits: m indices, each log2(k*) bits. m = 8 and k* = 256 gives 64 bits = 8 bytes per vector.
symbols.u_j(.): The j-th slice of a vector (D/m numbers).
symbols.c_{j,i_j(y)}: The centroid of sub-quantizer j that the stored index i_j(y) points to.
symbols.d-hat(x,y): The estimated distance. The query is kept exact (asymmetric distance computation, ADC); for each sub-quantizer the distances from the query part to all k* centroids are computed once and stored in a table, so each database vector needs only m table lookups and additions.
symbols.w: Number of cells searched at query time (the paper's w). Larger w means higher recall and more candidates to scan; w = 1 scans only one list.

units.inputs: The vectors, the knobs k' (cells), m and k* (code size), and at query time the query x, w (cells to visit) and how many neighbours k are wanted. Training: k-means for the coarse quantizer and for each sub-quantizer on a learning set.
units.range: Search returns approximate neighbours, recall between 0 and 1. The estimated distance is a biased approximation of the true distance (the paper discusses a bias and a correction).

worked_example.setup: Invented random data, our small implementation in numpy (plain k-means, 15 iterations), computed by a local script (not published) It follows the IVFADC structure of Jegou et al. but is not their code and not a benchmark; random Gaussian data has no cluster structure, so recall is pessimistic compared with real embeddings, and with only 8 dimensions and 1 byte per vector the code is very coarse.
steps: Toy inputs (invented random data, seed 3): N = 400 vectors of dimension D = 8, drawn from a standard normal. Coarse quantizer: k' = 8 k-means centroids (15 iterations, ours). Product quantizer on the residuals: m = 2 sub-vectors of 4 numbers each, k* = 16 centroids per sub-quantizer, so code length = m*log2(k*) = 8 bits.

Index build (paper Sec. IV): each vector goes into the inverted list of its nearest coarse centroid; list sizes [51, 32, 55, 39, 64, 51, 62, 46]. Stored per vector: the id plus the PQ code of its residual r(y) = y - q_c(y).

Memory per vector in the toy: raw 32 bytes (8 floats x 4 bytes) vs code 1.0 bytes (+ id). Reconstruction error (mean squared, computed): 1.664 vs total variance 8.077 of the data, so the codes keep part of the information but not all.

Query (IVFADC): find the w nearest coarse centroids, build m lookup tables of distances from the query residual to each sub-centroid, then each candidate distance is the sum of m table entries (paper Eq. 31). The query itself is not quantised (asymmetric).

Recall@1 against brute force over 200 random queries (computed): w = 1: recall 0.2, mean candidates scanned 50.54 of 400; w = 2: recall 0.225, mean candidates scanned 102.14 of 400; w = 4: recall 0.205, mean candidates scanned 205.465 of 400; w = 8: recall 0.205, mean candidates scanned 400.0 of 400.

Scale arithmetic with the paper's typical setting (D = 128 SIFT, m = 8, k* = 256, id 4 bytes): 1,000,000 vectors need 512 MB raw (float32) vs 12 MB as ids + 8-byte codes (computed, ignores codebooks and list overhead).

blind_spots: Lossy: the code is an approximation, so the true nearest neighbour can be ranked wrongly. A common remedy (re-ranking the top candidates with the full vectors) costs memory or disk access, and is not part of the toy.

A neighbour that sits in a different cell from the query is missed unless w is large enough; points near cell borders are the usual victims. In our toy the recall stays near 0.2 for every w, because the PQ approximation error, not the cell choice, is the limit there (random 8-D data with a 1-byte code); raising w only raises the number of candidates scanned.
Training needs a representative learning set; if the data shifts later, codebooks go stale and quality drops until retraining.
The same product quantizer is shared by all cells (the paper chooses this for memory reasons and says it probably gives slightly worse results than one per cell).
Equal-energy sub-vectors are assumed; if some coordinates carry most of the variance, a rotation may be needed (the paper discusses this).
The paper's experiments use image descriptors (SIFT, GIST); how the trade-off looks for text embeddings with strong anisotropy is not shown there (unverified).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use IVF+PQ when the vectors do not fit in RAM or the corpus has tens of millions or more vectors, and a little recall can be traded for memory. HNSW (see HNSW) is usually faster and more accurate at the same recall but uses more memory because it keeps full vectors and links. For under ~10^5 vectors an exact scan is simpler. IVF alone (no PQ) keeps full vectors; PQ alone (no IVF) scans every code. Libraries such as Faiss implement these structures (the Faiss naming is not checked here).

source.cite: Jegou, H., Douze, M. & Schmid, C. (2011) Product Quantization for Nearest Neighbor Search. IEEE TPAMI 33(1):117-128, DOI 10.1109/TPAMI.2010.57 (HAL inria-00514462). Read in the HAL PDF: product quantizer (Eq. 8-11, k = (k*)^m, code length m log2 k*), SDC/ADC, IVFADC with residual coding (Eq. 28-31), inverted-list layout, parameters k' and w. The memory arithmetic and toy results are ours.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in the HAL PDF of the TPAMI paper): the formulas and structure above, the typical k' range, residual coding, ADC lookup tables, memory layout. Derived by us: the memory totals for 1M vectors and all toy numbers (invented random data). Not opened: the Faiss documentation, so the statement that Faiss implements these is unverified. The paper's own recall/timing tables were not reproduced.

units.name: Chunking (size, overlap, structure)
units.question: How does the way we cut documents change what can be retrieved?
units.formula_latex: T=S-O,\qquad n=\Big\lceil\frac{L-O}{S-O}\Big\rceil,\qquad \text{storage factor}\approx\frac{nS}{L}\approx\frac{S}{S-O},\qquad P(\text{fact of }f\text{ words stays whole})\approx\min\Big(1,\ \max\Big(0,\frac{S-f+1}{T}\Big)\Big)

symbols.L: The length of the document, here in words (tokens work the same way).
symbols.S: Chunk size: how many words one chunk holds. DPR and the original RAG paper both used disjoint 100-word blocks.
symbols.O: Overlap: how many words two neighbouring chunks share. It repeats text on purpose, so a sentence cut at one border sits whole in the next chunk.
symbols.T = S - O: The stride: how far the window moves from one chunk start to the next.
symbols.n: The number of chunks, which is also the number of vectors to embed and store. A ceiling because the last chunk may be partial.
symbols.storage factor: How many times the text is stored in total (about S/(S-O)). No overlap gives 1; 50% overlap gives about 2.
symbols.f: The length of the piece of evidence (a fact, a table row, a definition) that must stay together to be useful.
symbols.P(whole): The chance that a fact placed at a random position lies fully inside at least one chunk. If a fact is longer than the chunk it is 0. The formula is a close approximation: a fact fits when its start falls in a window of S - f + 1 positions out of every T; it is capped at 1. The exact enumeration in the worked example is the reference (for example 0.731 against 0.71 for S = 100, O = 0, f = 30).
symbols.structure-aware chunking: Cutting at natural borders (sentence, paragraph, heading, table) instead of at a fixed count, so a chunk is one unit of meaning. It changes where the cuts fall, not the formulas above.

units.inputs: The documents, a unit (characters, words, tokens, sentences), the chunk size S, the overlap O, and optional structure rules (split on headings or paragraphs first, then by size).
units.range: S >= 1 and 0 <= O < S. Storage factor between 1 and large values as O approaches S. P(whole) is a number between 0 and 1.

worked_example.setup: Invented: one 1000-word document, exact enumeration over fact positions, computed by a local script (not published) It counts only whether a fact is cut; it does not measure retrieval quality, which depends on the embedding model and the question.
steps: Toy setting (invented): one document of L = 1000 words; a fact that needs f consecutive words to stay together (f = 30 or f = 60). A chunk of S words starts every S - O words (O = overlap). The last chunk is moved to end at the document end. Numbers below are exact counts by enumeration over every start position of the fact.

Case A, the setting of DPR and the RAG paper: S = 100, O = 0 (disjoint 100-word blocks): 10 chunks, storage factor 1.0; a 30-word fact stays whole in one chunk with probability 0.731, a 60-word fact 0.436.
Case B, S = 100, O = 20: 13 chunks, storage factor 1.3; 30-word fact kept whole 0.898, 60-word fact 0.544. With O = 50: 19 chunks, storage 1.9, 30-word 1.0, 60-word 0.828.

Case C, bigger chunks, S = 200, O = 0: 5 chunks, storage 1.0; 30-word 0.881, 60-word 0.749. Fewer chunks and fewer cuts, but each chunk now carries twice as much unrelated text in its embedding (not computed here: that effect needs a real embedding model).
Case D, small chunks, S = 50, O = 0: 20 chunks; 30-word 0.433, 60-word 0.0 (a 60-word fact can never fit in a 50-word chunk, so it is 0). With O = 10: 25 chunks, 30-word 0.541.

blind_spots: Cut facts: whatever the settings, a fact can straddle a border; overlap reduces the chance but never makes it 0, and long evidence (a table, a multi-paragraph argument) may be longer than any chunk.

Lost context: a chunk such as 'It was founded in 1998.' no longer says what 'it' is. Contextual retrieval (adding LLM-written context to each chunk) and late chunking (embedding the whole document first, then pooling per chunk) target this; one 2025 comparison found contextual retrieval kept meaning better but cost more compute, and late chunking was cheaper but lost relevance and completeness (that is one small study, not a settled result).
Big chunks dilute the embedding with unrelated text; small chunks may lack the context needed to answer. The best size depends on the corpus and the questions and must be measured, not guessed.
Overlap multiplies storage and duplicates near-identical hits in the top-k list, which then need de-duplication.
Fixed-size chunking ignores document structure (tables, code, headings), so structure can be sliced in half.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Chunking decides what the retriever can find at all; everything later (BM25, dense search, rerankers, HNSW) works on the chunks you made. Use fixed-size windows with overlap as the baseline; move to structure-aware chunks when documents have clear headings, tables or code; consider contextual retrieval or late chunking when chunks lose meaning out of context. GraphRAG indexing (see MS Local/Global) chunks too, but then builds entities and communities on top.

Lewis, P. et al. (2020) Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. arXiv:2005.11401, Sec. 3, PDF p.4: 'Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, to make a total of 21M documents'. The exact enumeration in the example was re-run by a local script (not published) all chunk counts, storage factors and keep-probabilities are identical to a local script (not published) The general statements about dilution and lost context are common practice and were not tested here. The other 2025-2026 arXiv chunking studies were not opened; their claims are not used.

units.name: GraphRAG: entity linking
units.question: How does a question mention become a node in the graph?

symbols.m: A mention: a piece of text in the question or document (for example 'Scott Young') together with the words around it. The context is what lets the model choose between people with the same name.
symbols.e_i: A candidate entity: one node of the knowledge graph. BLINK describes it by its title and a short description ('[CLS] title [ENT] description [SEP]').
symbols.y_m, y_e: The vectors that two separate BERT encoders produce for the mention-in-context and for the entity. Entity vectors can be computed once and cached.
symbols.s(m, e_i) = y_m . y_ei: The bi-encoder score: the dot product of the two vectors. A big value means the entity description fits the mention in its context.
symbols.B: Batch size in training. The other B - 1 gold entities of the batch serve as negatives for each mention (in-batch negatives); BLINK adds hard negatives, the top-10 wrong predictions.
symbols.L(m_i, e_i): The training loss. It is small when the correct entity has a much higher score than the others in the batch, and large when a wrong entity scores higher.
symbols.top-k: The few candidates the bi-encoder keeps (found by fast nearest-neighbour search over all entity vectors, or from an alias table).
symbols.s_cross(m, e): The cross-encoder score: query context and entity description are read together in one transformer, then one linear layer gives a number. It is slower but more exact, so it is only used on the top-k.
symbols.e-hat: The chosen entity, the graph node the mention is linked to. If the best score is too low, a system may also answer 'no entity' (NIL); that is a design choice not shown in the formula.

units.inputs: A text (a user question or a document), a knowledge graph with names and descriptions for its entities, optionally an alias table, and a trained linker (mention detector, candidate generator, ranker).
units.range: Scores are unbounded real numbers; softmax turns them into probabilities between 0 and 1 over the candidate list. The output is one node id per mention or NIL.

worked_example.setup: Invented toy knowledge base and sentence, computed by a local script (not published) The cross-encoder logits and the batch score matrix are invented; no neural model was run. The first-stage score is word-count cosine, our stand-in for the dense bi-encoder.
steps: Toy inputs (invented): the sentence 'Scott Young scored twice for Cardiff on Saturday as the forward helped his club to a win.'; the mention 'Scott Young' (the ambiguous name comes from the survey's example, the texts are ours); a 4-entity knowledge base with a title and a one-sentence description each: {'E1': 'Scott Young (footballer)', 'E2': 'Scott Young (writer)', 'E3': 'Scott Young (musician)', 'E4': 'Cardiff City F.C.'}.
Step 1, mention detection: find the span 'Scott Young' (and 'Cardiff'). Done by hand here; real systems use a trained tagger.

Step 2, candidate generation: look the mention up in an alias table (invented): 'scott young' -> ['E1', 'E2', 'E3']. A dense retriever (BLINK's bi-encoder) can replace the table by comparing the mention-in-context vector with entity vectors.

Step 3, bi-encoder-style scoring (our simplification): word-count cosine between the sentence and 'title + description' for each candidate: {'E1': 0.348, 'E2': 0.161, 'E3': 0.182}; order ['E1', 'E3', 'E2'].

Step 4, cross-encoder re-ranking (invented logits, no model run): {'E1': 3.1, 'E2': -0.8, 'E3': -1.9}; softmax probabilities {'E1': 0.974, 'E2': 0.02, 'E3': 0.007}; linked entity = E1 (Scott Young (footballer)). BLINK ranks the bi-encoder candidates with a cross-encoder in the same way.
Contrast: a popularity-only baseline using invented prior counts {'E1': 20, 'E2': 70, 'E3': 10} would pick E2 (Scott Young (writer)), which is wrong for this sentence; the context decides.

Training loss, BLINK Eq. 4, on an invented 3x3 batch score matrix [[4.0, 1.0, 0.5], [0.2, 3.0, 1.1], [0.4, 0.9, 2.5]]: per-pair losses [0.077, 0.191, 0.281], mean 0.183. The loss is small where the gold entity (diagonal) has the highest score in its row.

blind_spots: Ambiguity without context: a short question such as 'Who is Scott Young?' has no context to separate the candidates, so any linker is guessing among them (popularity prior or ask the user).

Missing entities: if the correct node is not in the candidate list (alias table gap, bad spelling, a new entity not yet in the graph), the ranker cannot recover it; the system should be able to answer NIL instead of linking to the closest wrong node.
Errors propagate: a wrong link sends GraphRAG's graph traversal (k-hop, PageRank) to the wrong neighbourhood and every later step is built on it.

Descriptions matter: entities with no or poor descriptions are hard to score; BLINK's results are for Wikipedia-style entities with text (the zero-shot setting) and may not transfer to a company knowledge graph (unverified).
Cost: running a cross-encoder for each mention and each candidate adds delay per question.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use entity linking as the entry step of graph retrieval: it turns the question's mentions into start nodes for k-hop expansion or personalised PageRank. Plain vector search of chunks needs no linking but cannot follow edges. Local search in Microsoft GraphRAG finds start entities by embedding similarity (see MS Local/Global), which is a lightweight form of the candidate-generation step. The survey by Sevgili et al. splits the task into mention detection and entity disambiguation; BLINK is one two-stage disambiguation design.

source.cite: Wu, L., Petroni, F., Josifoski, M., Riedel, S. & Zettlemoyer, L. (2020) Scalable Zero-shot Entity Linking with Dense Entity Retrieval. EMNLP 2020, arXiv:1911.03814 (BLINK): bi-encoder, entity input format, dot-product score Eq. 3, in-batch loss Eq. 4, hard negatives, cross-encoder re-ranking read in the arXiv PDF. Sevgili, O. et al. (2020/2022) Neural Entity Linking: A Survey of Models Based on Deep Learning. arXiv:2006.00575 (Semantic Web journal): the split into mention detection and entity disambiguation, and the Scott Young example, read in the introduction only.

units.notes: Evidenced (read): BLINK's two-stage design, the scoring and loss equations, the input formats (Wu et al.); the mention-detection / disambiguation split (survey introduction). Not opened: the survey's body and its benchmark tables, so statements about the field's methods beyond the introduction are not taken from it. How GraphRAG systems use entity linking (start nodes for traversal) is our synthesis, not from these two papers. All toy data is invented, including the alias table and the prior counts.

units.name: GraphRAG: k-hop / BFS expansion
units.question: How far from the seed entities do we walk, and what does it cost?
units.formula_latex: N_k(S)=\{\,v : d(S,v)\le k\,\},\qquad d(S,v)=\min_{s\in S}\ \text{shortest path length from } s \text{ to } v,\qquad |N_k|\approx \sum_{i=0}^{k} \bar d^{\,i}\ \text{(our rough growth estimate, tree-like graphs only)}

symbols.S: The seed entities: the graph nodes that the query matched (for example by entity linking or embedding search). The walk starts here.
symbols.k: The number of hops (edges) we are allowed to walk away from the seeds. k = 0: the seeds only. k = 1: the seeds and their direct neighbours. The one knob of the method.
symbols.d(S, v): Distance of node v from the seed set: the smallest number of edges on any path from some seed to v. Breadth-first search (BFS) finds it by visiting nodes ring by ring.
symbols.N_k(S): The expanded set: every node whose distance is at most k. Its triples (edges between these nodes) are what we hand to the LLM as context.
symbols.|N_k|: How many nodes the expansion returns. This is the cost: more nodes means more tokens for the LLM and more noise.
symbols.d-bar: Average number of neighbours per node (average degree). In a graph with no hubs and few shared neighbours, each hop multiplies the frontier by about d-bar, so the set grows like a geometric series. Real graphs have hubs and loops, so this is only an upper-style estimate.
symbols.BFS ring: The nodes at exactly distance i. BFS visits ring 0 (seeds), then ring 1, then ring 2, and so on, never visiting a node twice.

units.inputs: A graph (nodes and edges), a set of seed nodes, and the hop limit k. Optional: edge direction, edge-type filter, a cap on the number of nodes.
units.range: |N_k| is between |S| and the number of nodes in the seeds' connected component; it never decreases when k grows. It is bounded above by the total node count.

worked_example.setup: Part 1 (toy, invented): 9 nodes A..I, 10 undirected edges: A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, C-E, D-F, E-G, F-H, G-H, H-I. Seed S = {A}. Part 2 (invented, computed): a random graph with 10,000 nodes and 30,000 edges (average degree about 6, seed 3), BFS from node 0.
steps: BFS from A. Ring 0: ['A']. Ring 1 (direct neighbours): ['B', 'C']. Ring 2: ['D', 'E']. Ring 3: ['F', 'G']. Ring 4: ['H'].
Cumulative sizes |N_k| for k = 0..4: [1, 3, 5, 7, 8]. The set grows with every hop (node I, at distance 5, is still outside k = 4).
Node D is reachable by two paths (A-B-D and A-C-D) but BFS counts it once, at distance 2. BFS only knows 'reached or not'; it does not say that D is better connected to the seed than F.

Growth on the larger random graph (average degree 6.00), cumulative nodes for k = 0..5: [1, 4, 18, 98, 567, 2872]. Each hop multiplies the set by about 4 to 6 here (ratios [4.5, 5.4, 5.8, 5.1]), close to the average degree, and it would flatten only when the 10,000 nodes run out.
Cost reading: with 2 hops we hand the LLM 18 nodes; with 4 hops 567; with 5 hops 2872 (at an assumed 50 tokens per node: 900, 28350 and 143600 tokens).

blind_spots: Explosion: the set grows roughly like (degree)^k, so 3 hops on a social-like or hub-heavy graph can return thousands of nodes. The LLM context is small, so most of the walk is wasted.

Hubs: one node with a huge degree (a country, a company, 'Python') pulls in all its neighbours and drowns the answer in unrelated facts. Typical remedies: degree caps, edge-type filters, ranking the nodes (see Personalized PageRank).
No ranking: every node inside k hops counts the same. A node linked to the seed by ten paths and a node linked by one path both appear once.

Wrong k either way: too small and a multi-hop answer is cut off, too large and the context is noise. Which k is best depends on the question and the graph (the best k is not known in advance; unverified for any specific benchmark).
Depends on the seeds: if entity linking picks the wrong seed node, the whole expansion starts in the wrong place.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use k-hop expansion as the simplest graph retrieval: small k (1 or 2), a sparse graph, and questions about the direct surroundings of an entity. Use Personalized PageRank when you want a ranked list that rewards nodes reachable through many short paths and damps far, thin ones. Use community summaries (Microsoft global search) when the question is about the whole corpus, not about one entity's neighbourhood. Vector search needs no graph and no seeds, but cannot follow a chain of relations.

source.cite: Xu, M. (2021) Understanding Graph Embedding Methods and Their Applications. SIAM Review 63(4), doi:10.1137/20M1386062 (Zotero AQMNUKM6), Sec. 2.2.2, PDF p.7: 'the k-hop neighborhood is defined as the set of vertices that are reachable from a source node in k hops or fewer (i.e., following a path with k edges or fewer in binary graphs)'. This matches N_k for one seed; for a seed set S we take the union, which is the min over seeds in d(S,v) (our one-line extension). BFS, which computes d ring by ring, is textbook (Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms, elementary graph algorithms; not re-opened here). The growth estimate d-bar^i is our own back-of-envelope reading (valid only for tree-like graphs).

units.notes: Evidenced 2026-10-08: the k-hop neighbourhood definition read in Xu 2021 (SIAM Review, Sec. 2.2.2, PDF p.7), a peer-reviewed survey rather than the first paper to define it. Ours: the extension to a seed set (min over seeds), the growth estimate (labelled as ours in the formula), and all counts, computed by a local script (not published) on invented graphs; the 9-node BFS was re-checked by a local script (not published) (identical). The random graph is a simple model without hubs, so real knowledge graphs will behave differently (usually worse, because of hubs).

units.name: GraphRAG: Personalized PageRank (HippoRAG)
units.question: How do we rank nodes by their closeness to the seeds through all paths?

symbols.pi: The answer: one number per node, its personalized PageRank. It is the long-run share of time a random walker spends on that node. The numbers add up to 1. A big number means: close to the seeds through many short paths.
symbols.s: The seed (restart) distribution: one number per node, adding up to 1. In HippoRAG every query node gets the same probability and all other nodes get 0. Here: node A gets 1.
symbols.alpha: The restart probability (the paper calls it the damping factor and sets 0.5; note the usual 'damping factor' in classic PageRank is the other way round, 1 - alpha). At each step the walker jumps back to a seed with probability alpha, or follows a random edge with probability 1 - alpha. Large alpha: stay near the seeds. Small alpha: wander far.
symbols.1 - alpha: The probability to keep walking along an edge at each step.
symbols.A: The adjacency matrix of the graph: A_uv = 1 if there is an edge between u and v, else 0. (Weights can be used instead of 1.)
symbols.P: The random-walk matrix. P_uv is the probability to step from u to v: 1 divided by the number of neighbours of u (or the edge weight over the total weight). Each row adds up to 1.
symbols.pi P: One walking step: the probability mass sitting on each node is split equally among its neighbours.
symbols.(I - (1-alpha)P)^-1: The closed form. It sums up all walks of every length, each walk of length t weighted by (1 - alpha)^t. This is why 'all paths' count, short ones the most.
symbols.power iteration: How we compute it in practice: start with pi = s and repeat pi <- alpha*s + (1-alpha)*pi*P until the numbers stop changing.

units.inputs: A graph (adjacency matrix A), seed nodes with their weights (the vector s), and the restart probability alpha. In HippoRAG the seeds are the query entities, optionally multiplied by node specificity 1/(number of passages containing the node), and the scores of passages are obtained by multiplying pi by the node-to-passage matrix.
units.range: Each pi value is between 0 and 1 and they add up to 1. Only the order (and relative size) is used; the values depend on graph size. Higher alpha concentrates mass on the seeds.

worked_example.setup: Toy graph (invented): 6 nodes A..F, 7 undirected edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, C-E, D-F, E-F. Seed: A only (s = [1,0,0,0,0,0]). Restart probability alpha = 0.5 (the value HippoRAG tuned). Computed with numpy by power iteration (200 steps) and checked against the closed form (max difference below 1e-12).
steps: Step 1: pi = 0.5*s + 0.5*pi*P = [0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]. Half the mass restarts at A, the other half goes to A's neighbours B and C.
Step 2: [0.6042, 0.125, 0.125, 0.1042, 0.0417, 0.0]. Mass now reaches D and E (two hops away).
Ranking: A > C > B > D > E > F. D has two short paths from A (via B and via C), so it beats E, which has only one (via C), although both are two hops away.

Effect of alpha: with alpha = 0.85 the vector is [0.8581, 0.0648, 0.065, 0.0082, 0.0033, 0.0007] (almost everything stays at A); with alpha = 0.15 it is [0.2788, 0.1655, 0.2062, 0.1661, 0.0957, 0.0877] (far node F gains).

blind_spots: Hubs and degree bias: a node with many edges collects probability from many walks, so it can outrank a node that is truly more relevant. HippoRAG tries to counter this with node specificity (an IDF-like weight on the seeds); that helps seeds, not hubs in the middle of the graph.

Garbage seeds in, garbage ranking out: if entity extraction or linking picks wrong query nodes, the whole walk starts in the wrong place; and missed edges (triples the LLM did not extract) cut the paths that carry the answer.
Scores are relative, not calibrated: the values depend on graph size, degree and alpha. There is no natural threshold for 'relevant'; you take the top-k.
alpha is a knob without a theory: HippoRAG tuned 0.5 on 100 MuSiQue training examples; the best value may differ on other corpora (unverified).
Cost: exact solving needs a matrix inverse; power iteration is fine for small graphs but needs care for graphs with millions of nodes (approximate push methods exist; not discussed here).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use Personalized PageRank when seeds are few and you want a soft, ranked expansion that rewards nodes connected by many paths and fades with distance (HippoRAG uses it for multi-hop passage retrieval in one step). Use k-hop BFS when you want a hard, cheap neighbourhood with no ranking. Use Microsoft's community-summary search for corpus-wide questions. Plain PageRank (no seeds) ranks global importance and ignores the query.

source.cite: Haveliwala, T. H. (2002) Topic-Sensitive PageRank. WWW 2002. Read in the author's PDF (www-cs-students.stanford.edu/~taherh/papers/topic-sensitive-pagerank.pdf), Sec. 2, Eq. (5), PDF p.2: Rank = (1 - alpha) M x Rank + alpha p, with M the column-stochastic link matrix, p a non-uniform personalization vector and alpha the bias (teleport) factor; PDF p.4: alpha = 1 puts all score on the bias set, alpha -> 0 makes it irrelevant; the paper used alpha = 0.25. Our row-vector form pi = alpha s + (1 - alpha) pi P is the same equation transposed (M = P^T); the closed form is plain algebra on it. Gutierrez, B. J., Shu, Y., Gu, Y., Yasunaga, M., Su, Y. (2024) HippoRAG, arXiv:2405.14831 (NeurIPS 2024; Zotero DR6M6LNR): Sec. 2.2, PDF p.5: PPR over the KG with a personalized distribution in which 'each query node has equal probability and all other nodes have a probability of zero', node specificity, passage scores via the node-passage matrix; Sec. 3.4, PDF p.6: 'the PPR damping factor at 0.5, which determines the probability that PPR will restart a random walk from the query nodes'. Page et al. 1999 and Jeh & Widom 2003 were not opened (Stanford InfoLab server returned HTTP 500 on 2026-10-08).

units.notes: Evidenced 2026-10-08: the PPR equation read in Haveliwala 2002 (Eq. 5, alpha = teleport/restart weight on the personalization vector, same role as our alpha) and HippoRAG's seeds (equal mass on query nodes) and restart probability 0.5 read in arXiv:2405.14831 (Sec. 2.2, Sec. 3.4). Ours: the closed form (algebra) and the invented 6-node graph. Numbers computed in a local script (not published) and re-checked by power iteration in a local script (not published) (identical for alpha = 0.5, 0.85, 0.15).

units.name: GraphRAG: community detection (Leiden) and modularity
units.question: How do we cut the graph into topic groups?

symbols.Q_gamma: The quality score of one way of cutting the graph into groups (a partition). Higher means the groups look more like real clusters. Leiden tries to find the partition with the highest Q.
symbols.c: One community: one group of nodes. The sum runs over all groups, so every group adds its own term.
symbols.m: The total number of edges in the whole graph. It is a fixed number for a given graph.
symbols.e_c: The number of edges that have both ends inside group c. More inside edges mean a tighter group. (The paper writes the same formula with 1/(2m) and counts each inside edge twice, shown as e~_c = 2 e_c; both forms give the same number.)
symbols.K_c: The sum of the degrees of the nodes in group c. The degree of a node is how many edges touch it. K_c tells how many edge ends sit in the group.
symbols.K_c / 2m: The share of all edge ends that lie in group c. If edges were wired at random with the same degrees (the configuration model), the chance that a random edge end falls in c is this share.
symbols.(K_c / 2m)^2: The expected share of edges that would fall inside c by pure chance. We subtract it from the real share e_c / m: modularity rewards a group only for being denser than chance.
symbols.gamma: The resolution knob, gamma > 0. Large gamma punishes big groups more and gives many small communities; small gamma gives few big communities. gamma = 1 is the classic modularity.
symbols.Leiden phases: Leiden repeats three steps. (1) Local moving: each node moves to the neighbouring group that raises Q most. (2) Refinement: each group is split into sub-groups that are well connected inside. (3) Aggregation: each sub-group becomes one node, and the steps repeat on the smaller graph. The refinement step is what makes every community connected.

units.inputs: An undirected graph (in GraphRAG: entities as nodes, extracted relations as edges, optionally with edge weights), the resolution gamma, and a random seed (the algorithm is randomised).
units.range: For gamma = 1 the classic modularity lies between -1/2 and 1 (up to 1 only in the limit; real graphs with clear clusters often give about 0.3 to 0.7, a rule of thumb that is not from this paper). Q = 0 for one community that holds the whole graph.

worked_example.setup: Toy graph (invented): 6 nodes A..F, 7 edges. Triangle A-B-C, triangle D-E-F, and one bridge edge C-D. m = 7. Degrees: A=2, B=2, C=3, D=3, E=2, F=2. gamma = 1. We score three partitions with the formula (Python, a local script (not published) This scores partitions; it is not a run of Leiden itself.
steps: Partition {A,B,C} and {D,E,F}. For each group: e_c = 3 inside edges, K_c = 2+2+3 = 7. Share of real edges: 3/7 = 0.4286. Chance share: (7/14)^2 = 0.25. Each group adds 0.4286 - 0.25 = 0.1786. Q = 2 x 0.1786 = 0.3571.
Everything in one group: e_c = 7, K_c = 14, so Q = 7/7 - (14/14)^2 = 0. A single big group is no better than chance, by definition.
Every node alone: no inside edges, so each group adds only -(deg/14)^2; Q = -0.1735. Splitting too much is punished.

Resolution: with gamma = 2 the same two-triangle partition scores Q = -0.1429. A larger gamma raises the price of every group, so the same cut looks worse and the optimiser will prefer smaller groups.

What 'disconnected' means (second toy, invented): node b links a, c and the clique x1,x2,x3. Partition {a,b,c},{x1,x2,x3} has Q = 0.1172. If b alone moved into the x-group, {a,c} would have no edge between them (we check it in code: connected = False) and Q would be -0.0312. Here Q falls, so this exact move would not happen; it only shows what a disconnected community is. Q has no connectivity term, which is why Louvain can end with such communities on real networks (the paper measured up to 16% disconnected) and why Leiden adds the refinement step.

blind_spots: Modularity has a resolution limit (the paper cites it): in a large graph, modularity cannot see small communities, even clear ones; a good Q does not prove that the groups are meaningful topics.
The result is random: different seeds give different partitions, and gamma changes the number of groups. A GraphRAG index built once keeps one such cut; the summaries on top inherit it.

Leiden guarantees that communities are connected; it does not guarantee that a community is about one topic. In an LLM-extracted graph, noisy or duplicate entities and hub nodes (very high degree) pull unrelated nodes into one group.

Each community still needs an LLM summary (GraphRAG), which costs tokens at index time; Leiden itself is cheap. The paper's claims about speed and quality are on its benchmark networks, not on knowledge graphs extracted by an LLM.
The toy numbers score hand-made partitions. They do not show what Leiden would find on a real graph.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use Leiden when you need a hierarchy of connected topic groups over an entity graph, as in Microsoft GraphRAG-style indexes (the use of Leiden there is stated in the GraphRAG literature; this session did not open that paper). Louvain is the older, similar method but can return badly connected or even disconnected communities. Label propagation is faster but less stable (unverified here). Simple k-hop expansion (see k_hop) needs no clustering but gives no global view. See ms_local_global for how communities are then used for global questions.

source.cite: Traag, V. A., Waltman, L. & van Eck, N. J. (2019) From Louvain to Leiden: guaranteeing well-connected communities. Scientific Reports 9, 5233. DOI 10.1038/s41598-019-41695-z. Read in the journal PDF: modularity Eq. 1 with the resolution parameter gamma, the abstract's claims (up to 25% of Louvain communities badly connected, up to 16% disconnected; Leiden communities guaranteed connected; faster and better partitions). The 3-phase description is from the paper's overview. Worked numbers are ours.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in the paper): modularity with resolution gamma, the description that Louvain can yield badly connected/disconnected communities (25%/16% figures from the abstract), and that Leiden guarantees connected communities. Derived by us: the equivalent per-community form Q = sum[e_c/m - gamma (K_c/2m)^2] (algebra from the paper's 1/(2m) form if e_c counts each edge twice; the paper's text defines e_c as 'number of edges', so the double-counting convention is our reading, and the printed numbers use the standard form). The two toy graphs are invented. Not opened: the Microsoft GraphRAG paper, so the claim that GraphRAG uses Leiden is cited from memory (unverified here). Script: a local script (not published)

units.name: GraphRAG: Microsoft local vs global search (map-reduce)
units.question: When do we search entities and when do we summarise communities?

symbols.q: The user's question. Global search is meant for corpus-wide questions such as 'What are the main themes in the dataset?'.
symbols.community: A group of closely related entities found by community detection (the paper uses the Leiden algorithm) on the entity graph. Communities are nested: a hierarchy from big root communities down to small leaf communities.
symbols.community summary: A report-style text the LLM writes once, at indexing time, for each community. Global search reads these instead of the raw documents. The paper's levels C0 (root, fewest) to C3 (leaf, most) decide how detailed they are.
symbols.chunk_i: A group of community summaries. The summaries are shuffled and cut into chunks of a fixed token size, so one chunk fits one LLM context window and relevant facts are spread over chunks.
symbols.Map: (r_i, h_i): For every chunk, in parallel, the LLM writes a partial answer r_i to the question and gives it a helpfulness score h_i between 0 and 100. An answer with score 0 is dropped.
symbols.Reduce: Sort the partial answers by h_i from highest to lowest, add them to a new context window until the token budget is full, and let the LLM write the final global answer from that context.
symbols.T_sum, T_chunk: T_sum = total tokens of all community summaries at the chosen level; T_chunk = token size of one chunk. The number of map calls is about T_sum / T_chunk, plus one reduce call. This is the cost, and it grows with the corpus.
symbols.local search: The other mode of Microsoft's GraphRAG (described in the GraphRAG docs, not in arXiv:2404.16130): from the question (and, optionally, the conversation history) find the semantically related entities by entity-description embedding; use them as entry points to collect candidate connected entities, relationships, covariates, community reports and the source text chunks linked to those entities; rank and filter these candidates to fit one context window of pre-defined size; one LLM call answers. It answers specific questions about named things.

units.inputs: Global: the question, the community summaries at one chosen level (C0..C3), chunk size, token budget for the reduce step. Local: the question, the entity embeddings, the graph, the linked text units.
units.range: Helpfulness scores 0 to 100 (set by the LLM, so noisy). The number of LLM calls is the number of chunks plus 1. No retrieval score is returned; the output is a generated answer.

worked_example.setup: Global search, invented numbers: 8 community summaries with token sizes and the helpfulness score the LLM would give a partial answer: C1: 900 tokens, h = 70, C2: 1200 tokens, h = 85, C3: 800 tokens, h = 0, C4: 1100 tokens, h = 40, C5: 700 tokens, h = 90, C6: 1000 tokens, h = 0, C7: 900 tokens, h = 55, C8: 600 tokens, h = 20. Chunk size 2000 tokens, each partial answer 150 tokens, reduce budget 450 tokens. To keep the example reproducible we do not shuffle, and we give each chunk the best h among its summaries (a simplification: in reality the LLM scores the partial answer it wrote).
steps: Total summary text: 7200 tokens. Stuffing all of it into one prompt would need 7200 tokens, which would still fit one window in this toy; for a real corpus the summaries total far more than any context window, which is why the map step splits them.

Map: pack summaries into chunks of at most 2000 tokens: chunk 1 = ['C1'] (900 tokens); chunk 2 = ['C2', 'C3'] (2000 tokens); chunk 3 = ['C4', 'C5'] (1800 tokens); chunk 4 = ['C6', 'C7'] (1900 tokens); chunk 5 = ['C8'] (600 tokens). That is 5 parallel LLM calls.
Each map call returns a partial answer and a score (h, simplified): chunk 1: h = 70, chunk 2: h = 85, chunk 3: h = 90, chunk 4: h = 55, chunk 5: h = 20. Scores of 0 are filtered out.

Reduce: sort the remaining answers by h: chunk 3 (h = 90), chunk 2 (h = 85), chunk 1 (h = 70), chunk 4 (h = 55), chunk 5 (h = 20). Add them until the 450-token budget is full: kept ['chunk 3', 'chunk 2', 'chunk 1'] using 450 tokens.

One final LLM call writes the global answer. Total LLM calls: 5 map + 1 reduce = 6 (the simple estimate ceil(T_sum / T_chunk) + 1 gives 5; it is a lower bound, because whole summaries do not split across chunks). Local search, by contrast, is 1 retrieval step plus 1 LLM call regardless of corpus size.

blind_spots: Cost and latency: global search calls the LLM once per chunk of summaries, so it grows with the corpus and the chosen level. Lower levels (more, finer communities) cost more calls.

Indexing cost: building the entity graph and writing every community summary takes many LLM calls before the first query (the paper treats this as the price of the index; amounts depend on the corpus and are not computed here).
Helpfulness scores come from the LLM itself, so they are noisy and not calibrated; a good partial answer can score low and be dropped in the reduce step.

Wrong tool for specific questions: for 'what is the phone number of X' global search throws away detail; local search or plain vector RAG fits better. For 'what are the main themes' vector RAG alone fails because the top-k chunks cover only a small part of the corpus (this is the motivation stated by the paper).

The paper's evidence is LLM-judged win rates on comprehensiveness and diversity over two datasets of about 1 million tokens; it is not a proof of factual accuracy, and the judge can be biased (the paper's own limitation discussion should be read before citing numbers).
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use global search for sensemaking over a whole corpus (themes, trends, 'what is going on in this data'). Use local search for questions about specific entities and their surroundings; it behaves like k-hop retrieval plus text units, with one LLM call. Use plain vector RAG for fact lookup in a few chunks. Use Personalized PageRank (HippoRAG) when you want ranked multi-hop passage retrieval without generating summaries.

source.cite: Edge, D., Trinh, H., Cheng, N., Bradley, J., Chao, A., Mody, A., Truitt, S., Metropolitansky, D., Ness, R. O., Larson, J. (2024) From Local to Global: A GraphRAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization. arXiv:2404.16130 (v2, Feb 2025). Sec. 3.1.6 'Community Summaries -> Community Answers -> Global Answer', PDF p.6: summaries 'randomly shuffled and divided into chunks of pre-specified token size'; map: intermediate answers in parallel with 'a score between 0-100 indicating how helpful', 'Answers with score 0 are filtered out'; reduce: 'sorted in descending order of helpfulness score and iteratively added into a new context window until the token limit is reached'. Levels C0-C3: Sec. 4, PDF p.8. Local search: Microsoft GraphRAG documentation, 'Local Search' page, https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/query/local_search/ (opened 2026-10-08): entity-description embedding to find entities, then connected entities, relationships, covariates, community reports and linked text units, prioritized and filtered into a single context window of pre-defined size. The call-count line is our arithmetic, not in either source.

units.notes: Evidenced 2026-10-08: the global map-reduce procedure (arXiv:2404.16130, Sec. 3.1.6, PDF p.6) and the local-search dataflow (GraphRAG docs page, opened 2026-10-08; docs change with releases). Ours: the call-count formula ceil(T_sum/T_chunk) + 1 (arithmetic derived from the procedure, a lower bound, ignores retries) and all example numbers, computed by a local script (not published) (packing re-checked by hand: 5 map calls + 1 reduce).

It answers specific questions about named things. (This mode is not described in arXiv:2404.16130 as read here; see notes.)

units.name: GraphRAG: G-Retriever PCST subgraph
units.question: How do we pick a small connected subgraph with high-value nodes?
units.formula_latex: \mathrm{prize}(n)=\begin{cases}k-i,& n\text{ is the top-}i\text{ node of }V_k\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\qquad S^{*}=\arg\max_{S\subseteq G,\ S\text{ connected}}\ \sum_{n\in V_S}\mathrm{prize}(n)+\sum_{e\in E_S}\mathrm{prize}(e)-\mathrm{cost}(S),\quad \mathrm{cost}(S)=|E_S|\cdot C_e

symbols.G: The whole text-attributed graph (nodes and edges that carry text, for example a knowledge graph around the question).
symbols.S: One candidate subgraph: a chosen set of nodes and the edges between them. S must be connected: you can walk from any chosen node to any other chosen node.
symbols.V_S, E_S: The nodes and the edges that sit inside the candidate S.
symbols.k: How many top-matching nodes (and, separately, edges) get a prize. A small number, such as 3 or 5.
symbols.V_k: The k nodes with the highest cosine similarity to the question.
symbols.i: The rank of a node among the top k, counted from 0 for the best (so the best node gets prize k, the next k-1, and the k-th node gets 1). Nodes outside the top k get 0.
symbols.prize(n), prize(e): The reward for including node n (or edge e). Relevant to the question = big reward. Edges get prizes in the same way; a prize of 0 means 'include only if it helps connect other things'.
symbols.C_e: The price of one edge, a knob you set. Large C_e: only a tiny subgraph pays off. Small C_e: a bigger subgraph is allowed. The paper uses C_e = 1 (SceneGraphs) and 0.5 (WebQSP).
symbols.cost(S): The total price of S: number of edges times C_e. It keeps the subgraph small enough to fit into the LLM prompt.
symbols.argmax: Choose the S with the highest total of prizes minus cost. This is the Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree problem; the paper solves it with a near-linear-time approximate algorithm.

units.inputs: A graph with node/edge text, an embedding of the question and of every node and edge text (cosine similarity), k for nodes and for edges, and the edge cost C_e.
units.range: The objective value can be negative or positive; there is no fixed range. The best value is at least the prize of the single best node (a one-node subgraph costs nothing, as long as the single node is a valid subgraph). The number of edges in the answer is at most nodes - 1 for a tree.

worked_example.setup: Toy graph (invented): 7 nodes A..G, 7 edges A-B, B-C, C-D, B-E, E-F, F-G, D-G. Invented cosine similarities to the query: A 0.91, F 0.83, C 0.77, B 0.40, D 0.20, E 0.12, G 0.05. k = 3 (nodes only; edge prizes are 0 to keep it small). Default C_e = 0.5 (the paper's WebQSP value). We solve the objective EXACTLY by brute force over all node subsets (Python, a local script (not published) The paper uses a fast approximate PCST solver; brute force is only possible because the toy is tiny.
steps: Prizes (paper Eq. 6, ranks counted from 0): A (top 0) = 3, F (top 1) = 2, C (top 2) = 1. All other nodes = 0.
A connected subgraph with n nodes needs at least n-1 edges (a tree), so its cost is (n-1) x C_e. Candidate values: {A} = 3; {A,B,C} = 3+0+1 - 2 C_e; {A,B,C,E,F} = 3+1+2 - 4 C_e.
Ce = 0.5: best subgraph {A,B,C,E,F}, prize 6, cost 2.0, value 4.0 (default; the result below)
Ce = 1.0: best subgraph {A}, prize 3, cost 0.0, value 3.0 (the single node A wins: every extra node costs more than it earns)
Ce = 2.0: best subgraph {A}, prize 3, cost 0.0, value 3.0
Ce = 4.0: best subgraph {A}, prize 3, cost 0.0, value 3.0
Note the 'Steiner' part: B has prize 0 but is included when C_e is low, because it is the bridge that joins A to C and F. A plain top-k pick would take A, F, C and leave them unconnected.

blind_spots: It depends entirely on the prizes: if cosine similarity ranks the wrong nodes at the top (a weak embedding), the tree connects the wrong nodes very efficiently.
C_e is a knob tuned per dataset (the paper sets 1 and 0.5 for two datasets and k = 3 / 5). A bad C_e gives a subgraph that is too small to hold the answer or too big for the prompt.
Only the top k nodes get a prize; relevant nodes ranked k+1 get 0 and are lost unless they lie on a path between prized nodes.
The objective is a tree-like trade-off; it has no notion of relation type or path meaning (compare path_scoring). A short connection through a hub node can win even if it is semantically weak.
Our toy is solved exactly; the paper's solver is approximate (near-linear time), so results on big graphs may differ from the exact optimum. The toy does not show that.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use PCST when the answer needs a small connected evidence subgraph and the whole neighbourhood is too big for the prompt (G-Retriever's setting). k-hop expansion (k_hop) takes everything within h steps with no size control; personalized PageRank scores nodes by diffusion but returns no connected, budgeted subgraph; path scoring (path_scoring) ranks single paths. PCST gives one subgraph and an explicit size price.

source.cite: He, X., Tian, Y., Sun, Y., Chawla, N. V., Laurent, T., LeCun, Y., Bresson, X. & Hooi, B. (2024) G-Retriever: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Textual Graph Understanding and Question Answering. arXiv:2402.07630. Read in the arXiv PDF: the prize assignment Eq. 6, the objective Eq. 7, cost Eq. 8 (|E_S| x C_e), the virtual-node trick for edge prizes, the near-linear-time solver, and the hyper-parameters (k = 3, C_e = 1 for SceneGraphs; k = 3 nodes, k = 5 edges, C_e = 0.5 for WebQSP). Worked numbers are ours.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in arXiv:2402.07630): Eq. 6-8, the C_e values and k values, the virtual-node trick and the near-linear solver claim. Derived by us: the claim that the cheapest connected subgraph on a node set is a tree with n-1 edges (true for non-negative edge cost and no edge prizes; with edge prizes the paper's virtual-node construction changes this), and all toy numbers. Prize ranks are counted from 0 so the best node gets k, our reading of 'descending from k down to 1'. The paper's solver (Hegde et al., near-linear) was not opened.
units.viz_why: A small graph with a highlighted tree; the idea is the trade-off between prizes and edge cost, which 2-D shows clearly.

units.name: GraphRAG: LightRAG dual-level retrieval
units.question: How do low-level (entity) and high-level (theme) keys combine?
units.formula_latex: C(q)=\{\,v_i \mid v_i\in V\wedge (v_i\in \mathcal N_v\vee v_i\in \mathcal N_e)\,\},\quad v=\operatorname{top-}k_{u\in V}\cos\big(\mathbf k^{(l)},\mathbf u\big),\quad e=\operatorname{top-}k_{r\in E}\cos\big(\mathbf k^{(g)},\mathbf r\big)

symbols.q: The user question. An LLM first reads it and pulls out two kinds of keywords.
symbols.k^(l): The local (low-level) query keywords: names of specific things in the question, such as 'bees'. They are turned into an embedding vector.
symbols.k^(g): The global (high-level) query keywords: themes or concepts in the question, such as 'food security'. They are also turned into an embedding vector.
symbols.V, E: The nodes (entities) and the edges (relations) of the knowledge graph built from the documents. In LightRAG each entity and each relation has a short text key stored in a vector database.
symbols.u, r: The vector of one entity key, and the vector of one relation key (the relation key holds theme words that describe the link).
symbols.cos: Cosine similarity between two vectors: 1 means same direction (very similar), 0 means unrelated. Local keywords are matched against entity keys; global keywords against relation keys.
symbols.top-k: Keep only the k best matches. The paper says it matches keywords through a vector database; the exact k is an implementation setting, not a formula in the paper (our reading).
symbols.N_v, N_e: The one-hop neighbours of the retrieved entities v and of the retrieved relations e (the nodes you reach by walking one edge). Adding them gives 'higher-order relatedness': context around the hit, not only the hit.
symbols.C(q): The final context set: the retrieved nodes and edges plus their one-hop neighbourhood. The text attached to these elements goes into the LLM prompt.

units.inputs: A question; the knowledge graph with a vector index over entity keys and relation keys; the LLM that extracts local and global keywords; k (how many matches per level).
units.range: Cosine scores lie between -1 and 1 (for typical text embeddings mostly 0 to 1). The context size is between the k seeds and the seeds plus every neighbour; there is no score range for the final set, because LightRAG's paper describes a set union, not a ranking formula.

worked_example.setup: Toy KG (invented): entities Bees, Hive, Honey, Pollination, Crops, Smoke with invented 2-D embeddings (axes are fake 'topic' axes); 5 relations Bees-Hive, Hive-Honey, Bees-Pollination, Pollination-Crops, Smoke-Hive with invented relation-key embeddings. Question: 'How do bees affect our food supply?' The LLM step is replaced by hand-set keyword vectors: local 'bees' = (0.95, 0.12), global 'food security' = (0.25, 0.97). k = 1 per level. Python: a local script (not published) The set-union-with-one-hop structure follows the paper; top-k = 1 and all vectors are our choices.
steps: Low level: cosine of the local keyword with every entity: Bees 1.000, Hive 0.959, Honey 0.790, Pollination 0.556, Crops 0.279, Smoke 0.941. Best entity: Bees (0.9998).

High level: cosine of the global keyword with every relation key: Bees-Hive 0.543, Hive-Honey 0.766, Bees-Pollination 0.998, Pollination-Crops 0.999, Smoke-Hive 0.147. Best relation: Pollination-Crops (0.9990).
Seed set = best entity plus both ends of the best relation = Bees, Crops, Pollination (3 nodes). Low-level search alone would have found only Bees; the high-level key brings in Pollination.
One-hop expansion (N_v and N_e): add every node that shares an edge with a seed. The context grows to 4 nodes: Bees, Crops, Hive, Pollination, with 3 relations between them.
Result: the prompt gets the texts of 4 nodes and 3 relations. Crops, the end of the food-supply story, is in the context only because the global key matched the Pollination-Crops relation.

blind_spots: Everything depends on the keyword-extraction LLM call. If it labels a theme as an entity (or the reverse), the wrong index is searched and the right relation is never matched.

One-hop expansion grows quickly around hub entities: a very connected node can flood the prompt with neighbours that are not relevant. The paper does not describe a cap in the part we read (unverified for the code).
Relation keys are short text produced at index time by an LLM; a poor summary of a link makes it unreachable from global keywords.

The paper's claims of better comprehensiveness and diversity come from LLM-judged comparisons (win rates on four datasets); we did not reproduce them, and the toy numbers here show only the mechanism.
No real ranking of the final set: the union is passed on, so the order of evidence and token budget are separate engineering choices.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use LightRAG-style dual retrieval when questions mix specific entities and broad themes and you want graph structure without community summaries. Compared with Microsoft GraphRAG (ms_local_global), LightRAG reports a cheaper path: no community reports to regenerate when data changes (the paper's argument; costs not re-measured here). Plain vector RAG matches chunks only; k-hop (k_hop) expands from entities but has no theme level.

source.cite: Guo, Z., Xia, L., Yu, Y., Ao, T. & Huang, C. (2024) LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation. arXiv:2410.05779. Read in the arXiv PDF (Sec. 'Dual-level retrieval paradigm'): low-level vs high-level retrieval definitions; steps (i) keyword extraction k^(l), k^(g), (ii) vector-database keyword matching to entities and relations, (iii) one-hop neighbours N_v and N_e with the set {v_i | v_i in V and (v_i in N_v or v_i in N_e)}. Top-k = 1, the vectors and the cosine ranking are our toy choices.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in arXiv:2410.05779): the two retrieval levels, the three steps, the one-hop neighbour set. Not in the paper (our choices, flagged): cosine as the matching score, k = 1, the toy vectors. The paper's formula-like content is a set definition, so we show a union, not a ranking score. The paper's win-rate results were not examined in detail.
units.viz_why: A small graph and a 2-D keyword plane; the point is the two keys and the one-hop ring, which 2-D shows well.

units.name: GraphRAG: path scoring
units.question: How do we score a multi-hop path as evidence?

symbols.S(v): The 'resource' that node v holds. Think of water poured at the start node that flows along edges: nodes close to the start get a lot, far nodes get very little.
symbols.v_start: The first node of the path (a node retrieved for the question). It starts with S = 1; every other node starts with 0.
symbols.N(., v_i): The nodes that have an edge pointing into v_i: the nodes that can pass resource to v_i.
symbols.N(v_j, .): The nodes that v_j points to. Its size |N(v_j, .)| is the out-degree of v_j. A node splits its resource equally among its out-neighbours, so a hub with many out-edges passes only a small share to each.
symbols.alpha: The decay rate, between 0 and 1. Every step along an edge multiplies the resource by alpha, so longer paths get less. The paper's experiments use alpha = 0.7.
symbols.theta: The pruning threshold. If a node's per-neighbour share is below theta, the walk stops there (early stopping). This keeps the search cheap.
symbols.P, V_P, E_P: One path P from start to end. V_P is the list of its nodes and E_P the list of its edges; |E_P| is the number of edges (the hop count).
symbols.S(P): The reliability of the path: the paper's Eq. 4 adds up the resources of the nodes on the path and divides by the number of edges. Higher means a more reliable path. The paper then puts the highest-scored paths into the prompt.

units.inputs: A directed indexing graph, the retrieved start and end nodes, alpha, theta, and how many top paths to keep per node pair.
units.range: S(v) lies between 0 and 1 (resource starts at 1 and each step keeps at most alpha < 1 of it). S(P) is a positive number; with a start node worth 1 and a few nodes after it, typical values are below about 1. There is no fixed upper bound.

worked_example.setup: Toy directed graph (invented): s->a, s->b, a->t, b->c, c->t. alpha = 0.7 (the paper's experimental value), theta = 0.05 (our choice; the early stop never triggers here). Nodes are updated once, in topological order (the toy has no cycles; the paper's rule 'update at most once' is what we mirror). Two candidate paths from s to t: P1 = s-a-t (2 edges) and P2 = s-b-c-t (3 edges). Python: a local script (not published)
steps: Start: S(s) = 1. Node s has 2 out-neighbours (a, b), so each gets alpha x 1 / 2 = 0.7 / 2 = 0.35. S(a) = 0.3500, S(b) = 0.3500.
Node b has 1 out-neighbour (c): S(c) = 0.7 x 0.35 / 1 = 0.2450.
Node t receives from a and from c: S(t) = 0.7 x 0.35 / 1 + 0.7 x 0.245 / 1 = 0.245 + 0.1715 = 0.4165.

The shorter path scores higher (0.8832 vs 0.6705): decay and the division by hop count both favour short, direct connections. Note that Eq. 4 sums over nodes but divides by the edge count, exactly as printed in the paper; we followed the printed form.

blind_spots: It is a prior about structure, not meaning: S(P) uses only graph shape (degree, distance). A long but highly relevant chain loses to a short irrelevant one. The edge text and the question do not enter the score.
Hubs dilute: a node with many out-edges passes only 1/degree of its resource to each neighbour, so the path through a hub looks weak even when the hub is the real connector.

alpha and theta change the scores. In the toy (computed) alpha = 0.3 gives S(P1) = 0.5975 and S(P2) = 0.4133, alpha = 1.0 gives 1.25 and 1.0; the same ranking, very different scales, so any cut-off on S(P) must be tuned per graph (the paper fixes alpha = 0.7, N = 40, K = 15 in its experiments).

Because Eq. 4 includes S(v_start) = 1 in every sum, and divides by edges, the score is not a probability and cannot be compared across different start nodes without care (our reading; the paper does not discuss this).
The paper's gains are measured with LLM-judged comparisons on its own datasets; this session did not re-run them.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use path scoring when the evidence is a chain of relations (multi-hop questions) and the prompt can hold a few paths, not a whole subgraph. PCST (pcst_gretriever) returns one connected subgraph with a size price; personalized PageRank (personalized_pagerank) scores single nodes by diffusion; k-hop (k_hop) takes everything within h steps. PathRAG's flow is a resource-allocation relative of PageRank-style diffusion but stops early and ranks paths, not nodes.

source.cite: Chen, B., Guo, Z., Yang, Z., Chen, Y., Chen, J., Liu, Z., Shi, C. & Yang, C. (2025) PathRAG: Pruning Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation with Relational Paths. arXiv:2502.14902. Read in the arXiv PDF (section 'Path Retrieval'): resource propagation Eq. 2, early stopping Eq. 3, path reliability Eq. 4, and the settings N = 40, K = 15, alpha = 0.7. Worked numbers are ours.

units.notes: Evidenced (read in arXiv:2502.14902): Eq. 2-4 and the experimental values alpha = 0.7, N = 40, K = 15. Derived by us: the toy graph and all numbers; the topological update order (the paper says 'update at most once' without a toy). The seed names no specific source; PathRAG was chosen as the closest primary source for scoring a path as evidence. Other path-scoring methods (e.g. relation-path ranking in KG QA such as Path-based KGQA / Think-on-Graph) were not opened.
units.viz_why: A tiny directed graph with resource bars; the idea is flow and decay along a few edges, which 2-D shows clearly.

units.name: GraphRAG: combining graph and vector scores
units.question: How do we merge graph and vector evidence into one ranking?
units.formula_latex: s(d)=\lambda\,\phi\big(s_{vec}(q,d)\big)+(1-\lambda)\,\phi\big(s_{graph}(q,d)\big),\quad \phi(x)=\frac{x-\min x}{\max x-\min x},\quad s_{graph}=\frac{1}{1+h(q,d)}\ \text{(our construction)}\qquad\text{(HybridRAG itself: } C=C_{vec}\,\Vert\,C_{graph}\text{, vector context first)}

symbols.d: One candidate piece of evidence: a text chunk (or a node with its text) that could go into the prompt.
symbols.s_vec(q,d): The vector score: how close the question and the chunk are in embedding space, usually cosine similarity. It captures 'sounds like'.
symbols.s_graph(q,d): The graph score: how well the chunk fits the question through the knowledge graph. In our toy it is 1/(1+hops): 1 when the chunk's entity is the question's entity, 1/2 when it is one edge away, 1/3 for two edges. Real systems may use PageRank, path scores or community membership instead.
symbols.h(q,d): The number of hops (edges) between the entity found in the question and the entity of chunk d. It is our simple stand-in for 'graph closeness'.
symbols.phi: Min-max normalisation: shift and scale one score list so its smallest value becomes 0 and its largest becomes 1. It puts the two signals on the same scale before mixing.
symbols.lambda: The mixing knob between 0 and 1. lambda = 1 uses only vector scores; lambda = 0 uses only graph scores; 0.5 weighs them equally.
symbols.C_vec, C_graph: In HybridRAG (the paper) the two retrievers each return a context; the contexts are concatenated, the VectorRAG context first and the GraphRAG context after it, and sent to the LLM (Sec. 4.4). There is no mixed score.

units.inputs: For each candidate chunk: a vector score and a graph score for the same question; the weight lambda; a normaliser.
units.range: With min-max normalisation and lambda in [0,1], every fused score lies in [0, 1]. The fused value has no probability meaning; only the order matters.

worked_example.setup: Toy numbers (invented): 5 chunks c1..c5 with vector cosines and graph hops as in the steps below, lambda = 0.6, graph score = 1/(1+hops) (our choice), min-max normalisation. Python: a local script (not published) This is a weighted score fusion in the style of convex fusion (see convex_fusion), applied to a vector signal and a graph signal; HybridRAG as published concatenates contexts instead.
steps: Inputs (invented toy): five chunks. Vector cosine to the question: c1 0.82, c2 0.78, c3 0.55, c4 0.50, c5 0.30. Graph hops from the question's entity to each chunk's entity: c1 3, c2 2, c3 1, c4 0, c5 1. Graph score = 1 / (1 + hops): c1 0.250, c2 0.333, c3 0.500, c4 1.000, c5 0.500.

Min-max normalise each signal to [0, 1] (so a difference in scale cannot decide the ranking). Vector: c1 1.000, c2 0.923, c3 0.481, c4 0.385, c5 0.000. Graph: c1 0.000, c2 0.111, c3 0.333, c4 1.000, c5 0.333.
Fuse with lambda = 0.6: score = 0.6 x vector + 0.4 x graph. c1 0.6000, c2 0.5983, c3 0.4218, c4 0.6308, c5 0.1333. Ranking: c4 > c1 > c2 > c3 > c5.

Compare: vector alone ranks c1 > c2 > c3 > c4 > c5; graph alone ranks c4 > c3 > c5 > c2 > c1 . The fused list puts c4 first although it is only 4th by vector score, because its graph score is the maximum (0 hops); c1 is a close second (0.6308 vs 0.6000).

HybridRAG-style concatenation (what the paper does): take the top 2 from the vector list (c1, c2) and the top 2 from the graph list (c4, c3) and give the LLM their union: c1, c2, c4, c3 (4 pieces of context, no single ranking).

Why normalise: without it, putting the same graph score on a 0-100 scale instead of 0-1 gives ranking c4 > c3 > c5 > c2 > c1, versus c4 > c1 > c2 > c3 > c5 with min-max. The graph signal then simply drowns the vector signal.

blind_spots: The paper we opened (HybridRAG) does not define a mixed score at all: it joins two retrieved contexts. The weighted-sum formula is a common engineering pattern that we borrowed from convex fusion; it is not claimed by HybridRAG.
The graph score is not calibrated like cosine: 1/(1+hops), PageRank and path scores live on different scales, and min-max is sensitive to one outlier in either list (see convex_fusion).
lambda has no universal value; it must be tuned on labelled questions. A fixed lambda is wrong for questions where the graph is irrelevant (no entity found) or where vector search fails.

If the graph is wrong (extraction errors, missing links), the graph score pushes bad chunks up with high confidence. HybridRAG's own results show that combining contexts can lower context precision (0.79 for HybridRAG vs 0.96 for GraphRAG and 0.84 for VectorRAG on their financial-report data) while raising answer relevancy (0.96).
Our toy has 5 invented chunks; it shows how the mixing works, not how much it helps.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use a weighted fusion when you have one scalar graph score per chunk and labelled data to tune lambda. Use rank fusion (rrf_fusion) when the scores are on incomparable scales and you cannot tune. Use plain concatenation (HybridRAG) when you want both contexts in the prompt and the LLM can handle a longer context. Use personalized PageRank (personalized_pagerank) or path scoring (path_scoring) to produce the graph score itself.

source.cite: Sarmah, B., Hall, B., Rao, R., Patel, S., Pasquali, S. & Mehta, D. Read 2026-10-08 in the arXiv PDF: Sec. 2.3.1, PDF p.3-4 ('amalgamation of these two contexts'; 'This combined context is then utilized as input for a LLM'); Sec. 4.4, PDF p.7 ('The context from VectorRAG is appended first, followed by the context from GraphRAG'); graph retrieval there is a depth-first search 'constrained by a depth of one' (PDF p.7). The paper defines no weighted sum or score fusion. Weighted-sum form: our construction, after Bruch et al. 2022 (arXiv:2210.11934, read for the convex_fusion part). Worked numbers are ours.

units.notes: Still inferred after the 2026-10-08 check: HybridRAG combines the two contexts by ordered concatenation (vector first; Sec. 2.3.1 and 4.4), and it does NOT define a weighted sum. The weighted-sum formula, the 1/(1+hops) graph score and the toy numbers are ours (an engineering pattern, not a published result). Example re-checked by a local script (not published) fused scores 0.6000, 0.5983, 0.4218, 0.6308, 0.1333 (identical).
