units.name: Production: semantic caching
units.question: When can an earlier answer serve a new question?
units.formula_latex: \text{serve cached answer if }\max_{i}\cos\big(\mathbf e(q),\mathbf e(q_i)\big)\ge\tau;\qquad \bar C=C_{emb}+(1-h)\,C_{LLM},\quad \text{saving}=1-\frac{\bar C}{C_{LLM}}

symbols.q: The new question that has just arrived.
symbols.q_i: A question that was answered earlier and stored in the cache together with its answer.
symbols.e(.): The embedding model: it turns a question into a vector so that questions with similar meaning get vectors that point the same way.
symbols.cos: Cosine similarity between two vectors: 1 means the same direction (same meaning, as far as the embedding sees it), 0 unrelated.
symbols.max over i: We compare the new question with every stored question and look only at the best match.
symbols.tau: The similarity threshold. If the best cosine is at least tau, the cached answer is returned without calling the LLM; otherwise the LLM is called and its new answer is stored. A high tau (0.95) is safe but gets few hits; a low tau (0.80) gets many hits but can return a wrong answer.
symbols.h: The hit rate: the share of requests answered from the cache. It depends on how repetitive the traffic is and on tau.
symbols.C_emb: The cost of embedding the question and searching the cache. It is paid on every request, hit or not.
symbols.C_LLM: The cost of one full LLM call (retrieval, prompt, generation).
symbols.C-bar: The average cost per request with the cache. Each request pays C_emb; the misses (share 1-h) also pay C_LLM.
symbols.saving: The share of the LLM cost that the cache removes. It is positive only if the hit rate is bigger than C_emb / C_LLM (the break-even rate).

units.inputs: A stream of questions; an embedding model; a store of past (question, answer) pairs with a vector index; the threshold tau; cost figures for the embedding and the LLM call.
units.range: Cosine lies in [-1, 1]; useful thresholds are in the upper range, often about 0.85 to 0.98 (a rule of thumb, not from a paper; the right tau depends on the embedding model). The hit rate h is between 0 and 1; the saving is between 0 and 1 - C_emb / C_LLM.

worked_example.setup: Toy numbers (invented): cache holds 3 questions with invented 3-D vectors. Three new questions: a true paraphrase, a related question whose correct answer is different, and an unrelated one. tau = 0.95. Cost: C_LLM = $0.010, C_emb = $0.0001 per request (invented), hit rate h = 0.30 (invented). Python: a local script (not published) There is no model call in the toy; the vectors are hand-made, so the cosine values show the mechanics only.
steps: Best cosine of each new question against the cache (computed): 'How can I change my password?' = 0.9983 (best match: 'How do I reset my password?'); 'How do I delete my account?' = 0.9334 (best match: the same password question); 'Who won the 2022 World Cup?' = 0.4797.

Threshold sweep. tau = 0.80: paraphrase HIT (0.9983), related-but-different HIT (0.9334), unrelated miss (0.4797); tau = 0.90: paraphrase HIT (0.9983), related-but-different HIT (0.9334), unrelated miss (0.4797); tau = 0.95: paraphrase HIT (0.9983), related-but-different miss (0.9334), unrelated miss (0.4797); tau = 0.99: paraphrase HIT (0.9983), related-but-different miss (0.9334), unrelated miss (0.4797).

Reading the sweep: at tau = 0.95 the paraphrase is served from cache, the related-but-different question is not. At tau = 0.90 or lower the 'delete my account' question can hit the 'reset my password' answer: a wrong answer served with full confidence.

Cost: with h = 0.30, average cost = 0.0001 + 0.70 x 0.010 = $0.007100 per request, against $0.010 without a cache: a saving of 29.00%. Break-even hit rate = C_emb / C_LLM = 1.00%: below it the cache costs more than it saves.

blind_spots: Similar is not equal: the questions 'delete my account' and 'reset my password' are close in embedding space but need different answers. A threshold cannot see what is different. A wrong cached answer is returned confidently and may never be noticed.
The right tau depends on the embedding model and the domain; it must be tuned on labelled question pairs (same answer / different answer). A tau chosen on one model does not transfer to another.
Stale answers: the cache returns yesterday's answer after the documents changed. A time-to-live or an invalidation rule on document updates is needed (engineering practice).
Privacy and access: if answers depend on the user's permissions or private data, a shared cache can leak an answer to another user. Cache keys must include the user or tenant scope.
Our hit-rate and cost numbers are invented. In real traffic the hit rate may be much smaller; measure it before relying on any saving.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use a semantic cache for repetitive, low-risk, user-independent questions (FAQ-style). An exact-match cache is safer but misses paraphrases. KV / prompt caching (kv_prompt_cache) saves the cost of re-reading a repeated prefix but still calls the model and answers freshly. The semantic cache skips the model call completely, so it can also return a wrong answer; prompt caching cannot.

source.cite: Fu, B. & Feng, D. (2023) GPTCache: An Open-Source Semantic Cache for LLM Applications Enabling Faster Answers and Cost Savings. Proc. 3rd Workshop for NLP Open Source Software (NLP-OSS 2023), ACL Anthology 2023.nlposs-1.24. Read 2026-10-08: Sec. 3.5 'Similarity Evaluator', PDF p.4: 'GPTCache retrieves the Top-K most similar answers from its cache and uses a similarity evaluation function to determine if the cached answer matches the input query ... we eventually adopted the fine-tuned ALBERT model'; Sec. 3.7: the hit rate decides whether a cache pays off (no formula); Sec. 4: test pairs of three kinds, similar, opposite (related but not identical) and unrelated, which our toy mirrors. The paper gives no cosine-threshold equation and no cost formula. GPTCache (Zilliz) README, raw GitHub README opened 2026-10-08: a vector-store distance evaluator and the Config option similarity_threshold exist. The rule max cos >= tau is that configurable option, common practice; the cost formula is our arithmetic.

Ranges for tau are a rule of thumb and unverified. All toy vectors, costs and hit rates are invented; cosines 0.9983 / 0.9334 / 0.4797 and the 29% saving re-checked by a local script (not published) (identical).

units.name: Production: KV / prompt caching
units.question: What do we save when a prompt prefix repeats?
units.formula_latex: C_{cache}=P_{w}\,L+P_{in}\,U\;+\;(n-1)\big(P_{r}\,L+P_{in}\,U\big),\qquad C_{none}=n\,P_{in}\,(L+U),\qquad \text{KV bytes per token}=2\cdot d_{model}\cdot n_{layers}\cdot b

symbols.L: The length (in tokens) of the repeated prefix: the system prompt, the tool definitions, the retrieved documents that stay the same. Only the START of a prompt can be cached, so L counts tokens from the first token up to the last identical one.
symbols.U: The length of the unique part at the end: the new user question. It is paid at the normal input price every time.
symbols.n: The number of requests that reuse the same prefix while the cache entry is still alive (inside the time-to-live).
symbols.P_in: The normal price of one input token (the price per million tokens, divided by one million).
symbols.P_w: The price of writing the prefix into the cache on the first request. At Anthropic it is 1.25 x P_in for the 5-minute cache (from the pricing table we read).
symbols.P_r: The price of reading the prefix from the cache on a later request. In the table we read it is 0.1 x P_in for the model row we use.
symbols.C_cache, C_none: The total input cost of n requests with and without caching. The cache pays a small premium once (P_w - P_in) and saves (P_in - P_r) on every hit.
symbols.KV bytes per token: What the server stores per cached token: a key vector and a value vector (the factor 2) for every layer, each of size d_model, in b bytes per number. The vLLM paper gives the example 2 x 5120 x 40 x 2 = 819,200 bytes (about 800 KB) per token for OPT-13B in FP16.
symbols.prefix match: A request hits the cache only if its first tokens are exactly the same as a cached prefix. One changed token early on (a timestamp, a user name) breaks the match for everything after it.

units.inputs: The token lists of the requests (to find the shared prefix), the price per million input tokens, the cache write and read multipliers, the number of requests inside the cache lifetime, and the minimum cacheable length of the model.
units.range: Saving between 0 (no hits) and almost 1 - P_r/P_in (all later requests hit and the unique part is tiny). The prefix must reach the provider's minimum length to be cached at all (Anthropic documents model-specific minimums; OpenAI states 1,024 tokens).

worked_example.setup: Prices are from the Anthropic prompt-caching docs pricing table (opened 2026-10-08), row 'Claude Sonnet 4.5': input $3.00, 5-minute cache write $3.75, cache read $0.30 per million tokens. Scenario (invented): prefix L = 5,000 tokens, unique part U = 200 tokens, n = 10 requests within 5 minutes; input cost only (output tokens ignored). Python: a local script (not published) The prices may change; check the provider page.
steps: Without caching: 10 x 5,200 tokens x $3.00 / 1e6 = $0.15600.
With caching: the first request writes the prefix: (5,000 x 3.75 + 200 x 3.00) / 1e6 = $0.01935. Each of the other 9 requests reads it: (5,000 x 0.30 + 200 x 3.00) / 1e6 = $0.00210. Total = $0.03825.

Saving: 75.48% of the input cost. Break-even: the cache already pays off from request number 2, because the write premium (0.75 per million x 5,000) is smaller than one read saving (2.70 per million x 5,000).

Break it: if the prefix changes on every request (a timestamp at the top of the prompt), every request is a write and pays 1.25 x on the prefix: total $0.19350, which is 1.24 times the uncached cost. Order the prompt: stable parts first, volatile parts last.

What is cached inside the server: the KV tensors, not the text. For OPT-13B the vLLM paper computes 2 x 5,120 x 40 x 2 bytes = 819,200 bytes per token, so a 5,000-token prefix is about 4.1 GB of GPU memory (our multiplication; other models differ). This is why providers limit how long entries live.

Inside a self-hosted server, SGLang's RadixAttention keeps cached prefixes in a radix tree and evicts least-recently-used leaves. Toy (invented): 4 requests as token lists (SYS = system prompt, DOCx = document, Qx = question). Each new request reuses its longest shared prefix with an earlier one: 0, 3, 2 and 1 tokens; reused tokens = 6 of 15 total. The toy only measures longest common prefix; it does not build the radix tree.

blind_spots: It saves cost and latency, not correctness: the model is still called and answers freshly. It cannot reduce the cost of the unique tail or the output tokens.

Only an exact prefix counts. Reordering, a timestamp, a changed tool list or a different retrieved document at the top invalidates everything after it (both providers describe prefix matching; OpenAI states the whole rendered prefix must match).

Entries expire: the Anthropic docs say 5 minutes by default (refreshed on each hit) with a 1-hour option at higher write price; OpenAI documents its own retention rules that depend on model and settings. Sparse traffic gets no benefit and still pays the write premium.

A prefix shorter than the minimum cacheable length is not cached; no error is returned (Anthropic docs). Check the usage fields (cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens) to see what really happened.

In RAG the retrieved chunks usually sit after the system prompt and change per question, so only the static part (instructions, tool definitions, fixed documents) is cacheable. Our 5,000-token scenario is invented and optimistic.
Prices and multipliers differ by model and change over time; the numbers here are from one page on one date.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use prompt caching when many requests share a long identical prefix (a long system prompt, a fixed document, an agent's tool list). It is exact and safe. A semantic cache (semantic_cache) skips the model call altogether for similar questions but can return a wrong answer. Self-hosted engines get a similar effect from PagedAttention-style block sharing (vLLM) or RadixAttention (SGLang).

units.name: Production: monitoring and tracing (MLflow)
units.question: What do we log per stage to find failures and cost?
units.formula_latex: T=\sum_{s\in\text{stages}}t_s,\qquad C=\frac{(n_{in}-n_{cr})\,P_{in}+n_{cr}\,P_{cr}+n_{out}\,P_{out}}{10^{6}},\qquad p_{95}=\text{value at rank }\lceil 0.95\,N\rceil\text{ of sorted latencies}

symbols.span: One timed step of a request (embed the question, search the index, rerank, call the LLM). A trace is the tree or list of all spans of one request. Tracing tools record, for each span, its inputs, outputs, time and metadata (MLflow Tracing docs).
symbols.t_s: The time that stage s took, in milliseconds. In a sequential pipeline the request time T is their sum; spans that run in parallel need the longest one instead.
symbols.n_in: Input tokens the model reports for the call. In the OpenTelemetry GenAI convention (gen_ai.usage.input_tokens) this number includes the cached tokens.
symbols.n_cr: Input tokens that were read from the prompt cache (OpenTelemetry attribute gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens; Anthropic field cache_read_input_tokens). They are billed at the cheaper cache-read price.
symbols.n_out: Output tokens that the model generated, billed at the output price.
symbols.P_in, P_cr, P_out: Price per million input tokens, cache-read tokens and output tokens. From the provider's price page; they differ by model and change over time.
symbols.C: The cost of one LLM call. Summing it over spans gives the cost of the request; summing over requests gives the bill.
symbols.p95: The latency below which 95% of requests finish (nearest-rank method here). It shows the slow tail that the average hides.
symbols.gen_ai.operation.name: The OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute that names the kind of step. Documented values include chat, embeddings and retrieval (all marked 'Development' status when we read the spec on 2026-10-08).
symbols.top1 retrieval score: The similarity of the best retrieved chunk. A simple health signal: when it is low, the retriever probably found nothing useful, whatever the LLM then says.

units.inputs: For every request: a trace with one span per stage (name, start and end time, inputs, outputs, status) and, for LLM spans, token counts including cached tokens; for retrieval spans, the query, top_k and the scores; plus the price table.
units.range: Times are non-negative milliseconds; the cost is a non-negative dollar amount; p95 is at least p50. No score range: these are measurements, not a quality score.

worked_example.setup: One invented trace and ten invented requests. Trace: embed_query 40 ms, vector_search 85 ms (top_k = 5), rerank 210 ms, generate 1,450 ms with 3,200 input tokens of which 2,000 were cache reads, and 280 output tokens. Prices: Anthropic pricing-table row 'Claude Sonnet 4.5' (opened 2026-10-08): $3.00 input, $0.30 cache read, $15.00 output per million tokens; embedding and vector-search cost are ignored. Ten requests with invented latencies and top-1 retrieval scores. Python: a local script (not published)
steps: Trace time: 40 + 85 + 210 + 1,450 = 1785 ms. The generate span is 81.2% of it: that is where to look first for latency.

Cost of the generate call: input not cached = 3,200 - 2,000 = 1,200 tokens x $3.00; cache reads 2,000 x $0.30; output 280 x $15.00; sum / 1e6 = $0.008400. Without the cache reads it would be $0.013800 (all 3,200 input tokens at $3.00).

Ten requests: latencies [1650, 1720, 1580, 1790, 1610, 1700, 5200, 1660, 1740, 1690] ms. Median p50 = 1690 ms; p95 (nearest rank, rank 10 of 10) = 5200 ms; the mean is 2034 ms. The mean hides the one slow request (5200 ms), the p95 shows it.

Flags: slow requests (more than 2 x p50) = 1 (request #7). Requests with top-1 retrieval score below 0.5 = 2 (requests #6, #9): the answer quality there is suspect even though the latency is normal. These two lists need different fixes (infrastructure vs retrieval).

blind_spots: Logging inputs and outputs means logging user text and retrieved documents; that can include personal or secret data. Redact, sample, or restrict access (OpenTelemetry marks retrieved documents and query text as opt-in attributes).

Latency and token counts do not measure answer quality. A fast, cheap, wrong answer looks healthy on a latency dashboard; you still need evaluation (faithfulness, context relevance) on sampled traces.
Cost from token counts is only as good as the price table; prices change, cached-token pricing differs by provider, and the toy ignores embedding, vector-database and GPU costs.
The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions are marked 'Development' (not stable) in the page we read on 2026-10-08, and moved to their own repository; attribute names may change.
Tracing adds overhead and volume; at scale you sample, and a rare failure can be missed. The ten requests here are invented and show the arithmetic, not real traffic.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use tracing to find WHERE a request failed or was slow, per stage. Use offline evaluation (see the metric units, e.g. context precision, faithfulness) to judge WHAT quality you get on a labelled set. Use plain application logs when you only need errors. MLflow Tracing is OpenTelemetry-compatible (per its docs), so traces can go to MLflow or to any OpenTelemetry backend.

source.cite: MLflow Tracing documentation, mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/ (opened 2026-10-08): fully OpenTelemetry-compatible; captures inputs, outputs and metadata for each intermediate step; natively supports GenAI semantic conventions for export and ingestion. OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, spans page (github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai, docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md, opened 2026-10-08; the opentelemetry.io page now says it moved): gen_ai.operation.name values (chat, embeddings, retrieval, invoke_agent ...), gen_ai.usage.input_tokens includes cached tokens, gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens, gen_ai.retrieval.top_k, status Development. Prices: Anthropic prompt-caching docs pricing table (2026-10-08). Cost, percentile and flag arithmetic: ours.

units.name: Production: Intelligent Educator v2 end to end (RAG)
units.question: How does one question flow through the whole RAG stack, and what does each stage cost in recall, time and money?

symbols.q: The user's question, in the user's own words.
symbols.T: Query translation. An LLM rewrites q into a form the retriever handles better: several rewrites (multi-query / RAG-Fusion), sub-questions (decomposition), a more general question (step-back) or a hypothetical answer (HyDE).
symbols.{q_i}: The search queries that leave the translation stage. One question can become one query (nothing rewritten) or several.
symbols.route: Routing. Logical routing lets an LLM pick the data store (vector, relational, graph); semantic routing embeds the question and picks the closest prompt. With one corpus there is nothing to choose.
symbols.retrieve_20: First-stage search. Vector search and keyword search (BM25) each give a ranked list; Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges the lists by rank only. The top 20 candidates go on.
symbols.rerank_5: A cross-encoder reads the question and each of the 20 candidates together, scores them again, and keeps the best 5. It can only reorder what the first stage handed over.
symbols.C: The context: the kept passages, with their ids, put into the prompt.
symbols.LLM, a: Generation. The model answers only from C, cites passage ids, and says it does not know when C is not enough. a is the answer.
symbols.s_i: Success of stage i: the share of the cases in which the needed passages (or the right answer) survive that stage. A number between 0 and 1. For retrieval and rerank we measured it as gold-passage recall; for the other stages it is not measured yet.
symbols.prod_i s_i: The product of the stage successes. If every stage had to succeed and the stages were independent, the chance that the whole chain works is the product. Stages are NOT independent in practice, so treat the product as a rough upper-bound intuition, not a prediction.
symbols.c_i: Money spent in stage i (LLM tokens, embedding calls, reranker compute). Total cost is the sum.
symbols.t_i: Time spent in stage i. Total latency is the sum for stages that run one after the other; stages that run in parallel (vector and keyword search) count only the slower one.
symbols.cache: Caches (query, semantic, embedding, KV prefix) skip stages for repeated work. They change c_i and t_i, not the recall of a stage; a wrong cache hit is its own failure.
symbols.monitoring: One trace per request, one span per stage, with input, output, latency and tokens. It is how s_i, c_i and t_i get measured in production.

units.inputs: The success s_i of each stage (0 to 1; default 1 for stages with no data). In the real-example mode, also the question id; every stage's output is read from the real run files of the pack.
units.range: P_e2e lies in [0,1] and is never larger than the smallest s_i. Ten stages of 0.9 give 0.9^10 = 0.349 (toy).
units.higher_is_better: yes (for P_e2e); no for cost and latency

worked_example.setup: ONE real question from the demo pack (Presentations/_real-examples): q09, a bridge question: 'Who introduced the regularized regression technique that the multicollinearity article lists beside LASSO and elastic net as less sensitive to useless predictors, and in which year?' Gold answer: ridge regression, Hoerl and Kennard, 1970. Two gold passages are needed: p074 (Multicollinearity, names ridge regression) and p002 (Ridge regression, lead: Hoerl and Kennard 1970). Corpus: 138 Wikipedia passages, demo scale; NOT an evaluation of the thesis system. Stage numbers below are real runs; generation, caching and monitoring have no real data yet ('pending real data').
steps: 1 Translate (real LLM output, qwen3.7-plus, temperature 0): multi-query wrote 3 variants: 'regularized regression techniques compared to LASSO and elastic net for multicollinearity', 'who invented ridge regression and when was it introduced', 'history of ridge regression origin year and author'. Cost 85 prompt + 36 completion tokens = USD 0.000063 (at USD 0.276 / 1.101 per million tokens). Variant 2 puts p002 at rank 1 of its dense top-5 (original question: p002 not in dense top-5).
2 Route: the pack has one corpus, so there is no routing choice. Pending real data (a multi-store setup is not built).

3 Retrieve: BM25 ranks p074 first (score 34.75) and does not return p002 in its top 20. Dense cosine (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) ranks p074 3rd (0.5836) and p002 8th. The two gold passages have different rank patterns in the two lists, which is why we fuse.
4 Fuse: RRF (k=60) of the full BM25 and dense rankings puts p074 1st (0.0323) and p002 15th. Both gold passages are inside the top 20 that go on to the reranker.

5 Rerank: the cross-encoder scores the top 20: p074 4.83, p005 1.77, p006 1.60, p016 -0.55, p001 -1.21, p004 -2.00, p018 -2.10, p002 -2.48 (rank 8). Keeping 5 passages keeps p074 and drops p002: 1 of 2 gold passages survive.
6 Context: top 5 = p074, p005, p006, p016, p001. It names ridge regression (p074) but the year and the authors are in p002, which is not in the context.

7 Generate: pending real data (no answer run exists yet). Inferred from the passage text, not measured: an answer built only from this context can name ridge regression but not 'Hoerl and Kennard, 1970'; a good prompt should abstain on that part.
8 Cache and monitoring: pending real data (no latency or per-stage cost was measured, except the translation tokens in step 1).

9 Compounding on all 20 answerable questions (gold-passage recall, binary, computed from the runs): recall@20 after RRF = 0.975, recall@5 after rerank = 0.90, so the rerank stage keeps 0.90 / 0.975 = 0.9231 of what retrieval found. s = 1 x 1 x 0.975 x 0.9231 x 1 x 1 = 0.90 (stages with no data counted as 1; ours: the product rule). Toy break-it: six stages at 0.9 each give 0.9^6 = 0.531.

blind_spots: The product assumes independent stages. They are not: a bad rewrite changes what the retriever sees, a good reranker partly repairs a weak first stage. The product is an intuition, not a forecast (ours).
Stages with no measurement are counted as 1, which makes the product too optimistic. Generation, routing and caches are not measured here.
The numbers are demo scale: 138 passages, 20 scored questions; one question moves a rate by 0.05. They do not describe Intelligent Educator v2.
One question is an illustration. q09 is a bridge question and loses a gold passage at the rerank cut; a single-hop question would show a clean run.
Recall of gold passages is a proxy: other passages may also answer, and the gold labels were written by Claude from the text (lexical check only).
Latency adds only for sequential stages; parallel arms (vector and keyword search) cost the slower one, so a plain sum overstates it.
Caches change cost and latency, but a wrong semantic-cache hit returns a wrong answer without running any stage.
units.use_vs_neighbours: Use this unit to see the whole path and where recall is lost. For the details of one stage use its own unit: multi_query_rag_fusion, decomposition, step_back, hyde (translate); bm25, vector_similarity, hnsw, rrf_fusion (retrieve); cross_encoder, mmr (rerank); semantic_cache, kv_prompt_cache (cache); monitoring_tracing (trace). For the graph version use end_to_end_graphrag. The page 'RAG Production Stack' (Presentations/RAG Production Stack - 2026-10-08) tells the same flow with every step's problem, fix, and evidence; this unit does not duplicate it, it follows one real question through it.

units.name: Production: Intelligent Educator v2 end to end (GraphRAG)
units.question: How does one question flow through a GraphRAG stack, where does the graph add a passage, where does it lose one, and what does it cost?

symbols.q: The user's question, in the user's own words.
symbols.𝒢 (calligraphic G): The knowledge graph built at index time: nodes are entities, edges are typed relations, each node and edge points back to the passages it was extracted from. In the pack: 662 nodes and 762 edges from 138 passages.
symbols.link, S: Entity linking. The question is matched to graph nodes (whole-word string match first, then MiniLM embedding cosine of at least 0.55). S is the set of linked nodes, the seeds. A question with no seed is a miss.
symbols.PPR / k-hop: Expansion from the seeds. k-hop walks k edges out from S. Personalized PageRank (PPR) lets a random walker restart at the seeds with probability 0.5 and scores every node by how often it is visited. A passage scores the sum of the PPR scores of the nodes attached to it (a stand-in rule of ours).
symbols.passages_G: The passages ranked by that graph score. The top 5 go on.
symbols.dense_5: The top 5 passages of plain dense (cosine) search, as in the vector arm of the plain RAG stack.
symbols.assemble, C: Context assembly. Concatenation, vector first (the order HybridRAG uses): dense top 5, then the graph top 5 that are not already in it. C holds 5 to 10 passages.
symbols.community reports: Leiden groups the graph into communities (57 here); an LLM writes a short report for each of the 15 largest. Local search puts 5 of them into the context window; global search maps over all of them. They imitate Microsoft GraphRAG; they are not its code.
symbols.LLM, a: Generation. The model answers only from C, cites passage ids, and says the answer is not in the sources when C is not enough.
symbols.p_theta(G | q, 𝒢): G-Retrieval in the human's diagram: the probability of choosing the subgraph or passages G, given the question and the graph.
symbols.p_phi(a | q, G): G-Generation in the human's diagram: the probability of the answer a, given the question and the retrieved G.
symbols.gold: The passages a human-style label says are needed to answer the question (here written by Claude from the text). q10 has two: p015 and p006.
symbols.recall_C: The share of gold passages that are in C. A proxy: it says the evidence arrived, not that the answer is right.
symbols.cache and monitoring: Same layers as plain RAG, plus graph-specific work: extraction cached by chunk hash, community reports computed once at index time, and trace spans for linking, traversal and pruning. Not measured here.

units.inputs: The question id (default q10), the dense top-5 and the graph (PPR) top-5 passage ids, and the gold passage ids. Every list is read from the real run files of the pack; the number of passages taken from each arm can be changed.
units.range: recall_C lies in [0,1]. Concatenation can only add passages, so recall_C is never below recall of the vector top 5 (and never below the graph top 5). Context size grows with every added passage.
units.higher_is_better: yes for recall; no for context size, cost and latency

worked_example.setup: ONE real question from the demo pack (Presentations/_real-examples): q10, a bridge question: 'Which statistician popularised the method that, in the large p, small n case, selects at most n variables before it saturates, and in which year?' Gold answer: Robert Tibshirani popularised the lasso in 1996. Gold passages: p015 (lasso, at most n variables) and p006 (Tibshirani, 1996). Corpus: 138 Wikipedia passages, demo scale; NOT an evaluation of the thesis system. The graph was built by an LLM (qwen3.8-flash), 662 nodes, 762 edges. All numbers below are read from the pack's graph/ and answers/ files. Stages with no run (routing, cache, monitoring, per-stage latency) are marked 'pending real data'.
steps: 1 Entity linking (real): one seed only, the node 'large p, small n case' (string match, score 1.0). The embedding top-3 for this question has cosine at most 0.38, so the embedding step added nothing. One seed is a thin start, and it reaches 1 of 2 gold passages at hop 0 (p015).

2 Expansion (real, k-hop): hop 0 = 1 node, 1 passage (p015); hop 1 = 2 nodes ('penalty function'), still 1 passage; hop 2 adds the node 'lasso': 3 nodes, 10 passages, and p006 arrives. Both gold passages are inside 2 hops, the expansion touches 7.2% of the corpus.

3 Personalized PageRank (real): top nodes large p small n case 0.572, penalty function 0.288, lasso 0.082. Passage ranking: p015 1st (0.944), p005, p013, p006 4th (0.092), p012. Both gold passages are in the graph top 5. Dense search alone ranks them p006 2nd and p015 7th, so its top 5 holds only p006.

4 Community reports (real, local search): not run for q10 (local search was run for q09, q12, q16, q18). The reports exist (15 of 57 communities) but did not enter this question's context. Pending real data for q10.

5 Context assembly (real): dense top 5 = p068, p006, p002, p047, p075 (recall 0.5); graph top 5 = p015, p005, p013, p006, p012 (recall 1.0); concatenation = 9 passages, recall 1.0, 773 words against 461 for the dense top 5 (+68% on this question; +45% on average over 20 questions: 608 vs 419 words).

6 Generation (real, slice 4, arm C = dense top 5 + graph passages, qwen3.7-plus, temperature 0): the answer names lasso, Tibshirani and 1996 with citations [p015] and [p006]. Faithfulness 1.0, correctness 1.0, citation recall 1.0. Cost USD 0.000411, latency 4.39 s, 1213 prompt tokens. Honest comparison: arm B (RRF top 5, which already holds both gold passages for q10) gives the same answer for USD 0.000277 and 3.07 s. So on q10 the graph repaired the DENSE ranking; it did not beat hybrid RRF.

7 Failure case, q09 (real): 'Who introduced the technique that the multicollinearity article lists beside LASSO and elastic net ... and in which year?' Gold p074 and p002 (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970). All gold passages are reachable at hop 0 (6 seeds, 17 passages), and the PCST subgraph contains both. But the PPR passage score puts p074 1st and p002 11th, so the graph top 5 and the concatenation hold only p074 (recall 0.5). Arm C answers 'ridge regression [p074]', names Tikhonov from p001, and says the year is not in the sources: correctness 0.5, faithfulness 1.0, USD 0.000411. It does not invent 1970. Arm B refuses outright (correctness 0.0). Local search for q09 also contains only p074 of the two.

8 More failures (real, graph/entity_linking.json, khop.json): q13, q14 and q18 never reach their second gold passage within 3 hops (p051, p089, p026), so no ranking rule could fix them. 14 of 20 answerable questions reach all gold at hop 0, 17 within 3 hops.

9 Over the 20 answerable questions (real, computed in the pack): PPR alone is worse than dense: recall@5 0.775 and MRR 0.756 against 0.85 and 0.917. Concatenating dense and graph passages lifts gold recall from 0.85 to 0.875 (one gold passage in one question, q10) at about 45% more context. On the 12 answered questions: faithfulness A 0.47, B 0.94, C 0.97; cost per answer A USD 0.00011, B 0.00026, C 0.00034; latency about 3.7 s in every arm.
10 Cache and monitoring: pending real data (no cache run, no trace; the 3.7 s is one wall-clock call to a remote endpoint, not a pipeline latency).

blind_spots: PPR alone is worse than dense on this corpus (recall@5 0.775, MRR 0.756 vs 0.85 / 0.917); the graph helps only as an addition, and by one gold passage in one question out of 20.
q10 is chosen because the graph helps there (ours). Against hybrid RRF the gain disappears: arm B already held both gold passages and gave the same answer more cheaply.
Reachable is not retrieved: q09 reaches both gold passages at hop 0, yet the passage score ranks p002 11th. The passage rule (sum of node PPR scores) is a stand-in, other rules were not tried.

Some failures are structural: q13, q14 and q18 never reach their second gold passage within 3 hops (extraction missed or split the link). Linking is noisy: q10 has one seed, q04 links 'data', q05 links 'algorithm'.
The graph is small-world: by hop 3 an expansion touches about 65% of the corpus, so deep hops are no filter.

B versus C does NOT isolate the graph: C gets about 40% more prompt tokens, and B and C start from different first-stage lists (RRF vs dense). Faithfulness 0.94 vs 0.97 has a paired interval that contains 0.

Answer numbers: n = 12 questions, one run, temperature 0, LLM judges only (kappa 0.78 between two LLMs), no human labels; one question moves a mean by 0.08-0.11. Demo scale, not a benchmark and not an evaluation of Intelligent Educator v2.

Local and global search here imitate Microsoft GraphRAG (Edge et al. 2024) with simplified rules (estimated tokens, no claims, flat Leiden); they are not its code, and the 20/50/30 window proportions are ours.

The graph is LLM-extracted and unchecked against a human graph; near-duplicate nodes remain; every community report is LLM text. Index cost is real: USD 0.0273 extraction + 0.0085 reports for 138 passages, paid once, before any question.
